CPR and choking for every age, allergic reactions, bleeding, heart attack and stroke, a full babies-and-children section, snakes and marine life, and how to actually get help here. Checked against named medical authorities — see its own sources.

Checked hospitals with a 24-hour emergency department come first (children’s care first for a family), then straight-line distance. Closer places from OpenStreetMap follow, unchecked. The full screen has the rest of the country, what to do where nothing is listed, how people reach a hospital here, and your medical card.
Choose accommodation with strong recent reviews and 24-hour reception; a door that locks from the inside, and a padlock for hostel lockers, are worth it.

Consular help is free and is the right first call for a lost passport, an arrest, a death or a large-scale emergency. Find yours and save the address now — searching for it during the emergency is the part that goes wrong.
Do not apply a tight tourniquet, ice, alcohol or an electric shock.
Do not chase or try to kill the snake, and do not wait to “see if it was venomous”.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck out the venom.
Do not dismiss a minor scratch or a lick on broken skin — these can pass on rabies too.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled and filtered water is cheap and everywhere, with refill stations in most towns. Ice in cafés and restaurants is factory-made and generally safe.
Do not make them stand up or walk around.
Do not rub the area or rinse with fresh water — it can fire more stinging cells.
Do not scrub hard enough to bruise the tissue, and do not have the wound stitched closed straight away unless a doctor decides it is necessary — leave it open after washing.
Do not wait for symptoms to worsen before using adrenaline.
Do not wait to “see if the animal was sick”, and do not assume a calm or healthy-looking animal is safe.
Dress modestly at temples (shoulders and knees covered) and more conservatively in rural and Muslim-majority areas; it draws less attention and respects local custom.

For a stonefish or stingray wound, soak the area in water as hot as can be comfortably tolerated (around 45°C). A sea-urchin puncture is different: wash it with soap and water instead — do not use the hot-water method on that one.
Get out of the water. Douse the sting with vinegar for at least 30 seconds — many beaches keep a bottle for this.

Get to a clinic or hospital the same day for rabies post-exposure vaccination — do not wait for symptoms. Dog, cat, monkey and bat bites or scratches across this region can carry rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms begin but is nearly always preventable when treatment starts promptly.
Get to a hospital even if they improve — symptoms can return hours later.
Get to a hospital that can give antivenom as fast as possible, and call the emergency number on the way.

If an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) is available, use it at once into the outer thigh, then call emergency services.

If someone collapses and is not breathing normally, send someone to call the emergency number and fetch an AED, then start hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second, until help arrives.

Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint or sling.

In a serious emergency, call the number above. Show this screen to a local to ask for help. Tourist police often speak English. First-aid guidance here is general and does not replace professional medical care.
In an emergency, hospital emergency rooms and ambulances carry injectable adrenaline given by staff — reaching one fast matters more than finding a pharmacy.
Lay the person flat and raise their legs; if breathing is hard, let them sit up. A second dose may be needed after about 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
Lift off any tentacles with the edge of a card or a gloved hand.
Move out of the snake’s reach; keep the person calm and as still as possible — panic and movement speed venom through the body.
Note the snake’s colour, size and shape, or photograph it from a safe distance — it helps doctors choose the antivenom.
On the islands, take care at Full Moon-style parties: go with people you trust, mind your drink, and arrange your return boat or taxi in advance.
Public AEDs are not widely mapped in the region. You are most likely to find one at international airports, large shopping malls, five-star hotels and hospitals — ask staff or security.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts.
Rent a scooter only with the correct licence and a helmet — road injuries are the single biggest real risk to travellers here.
Show or speak these to hospital staff or anyone helping you. Works offline.
Show “I need a hospital” to a local (works offline)
Signs: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, widespread hives, or dizziness or collapse after a sting, food or medicine.
Street food is a highlight and safe when the stall is busy and food is cooked fresh in front of you. Peel your own fruit, and be cautious with reheated buffet dishes left standing.

Tell the clinic if the skin was broken, if a bat was involved, or if saliva reached your eyes, mouth or an open cut — these also need rabies immunoglobulin, not the vaccine alone.

Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos are, by global standards, among the safer places to travel solo — including for women. Ordinary city precautions apply; violent crime against tourists is rare and opportunistic theft is the main risk.
To try to buy one locally, ask the pharmacy of a large international hospital (for example Bumrungrad or Samitivej in Bangkok). Availability is not guaranteed — telephone ahead.
Treat any difficulty breathing, chest pain or collapse as life-threatening, start CPR if needed, and call for help — box jellyfish stings can kill within minutes.
Trust your instincts — it is always fine to be firm, say no, or walk away. Save the tourist-police and your embassy numbers offline before you need them.
Use booked ride apps (Grab, Bolt) or metered taxis rather than unmarked cars, especially at night, and check the plate before getting in. Share your live trip with someone you trust.

What to do first — then get to a hospital. General first aid, not a substitute for a doctor.
Eat where locals queue and food is cooked to order. Be extra careful with ice, salads and shellfish in rural areas and the hot season; peel your own fruit.
In Phnom Penh, bag-snatching from passing motorbikes is the main risk: wear bags across the body on the side away from the road, and keep your phone out of sight near traffic.
Tap water is not safe to drink. Stick to sealed bottled or filtered water and check the seal. Outside the cities, ask for drinks without ice unless you are sure it is commercial ice.
Use Grab or the PassApp for tuk-tuks and cars, so the fare and route are logged.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled water is widely sold and refill stations exist in tourist towns. Outside the main towns, ask for no ice unless you know it is commercial.
Freshly grilled and boiled dishes from busy stalls are safest. Avoid raw or fermented meat/fish dishes such as laap dib — they carry a real parasite risk. Peel fruit yourself.
Laos is very relaxed and low-crime, but towns wind down early — plan transport before dark, especially in rural areas where lighting and taxis are scarce.
On tubing or river days around Vang Vieng, be careful with alcohol near fast water; this is the main cause of traveller injuries.
Busy stalls with high turnover are safest — choose freshly cooked, steaming dishes. Go easy on raw herbs you cannot wash yourself and on shellfish in hot weather.
Carry bags on the pavement side and keep phones away from the kerb; snatch-thefts from passing motorbikes happen in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi.
Do not drink the tap water. Use bottled or filtered water; most hotels supply it free. Café and bia-hơi ice in cities is normally commercial ice and fine.
Use Grab (car or bike) in cities and insist on a helmet on bike taxis. Traffic is the main hazard — cross slowly and steadily so riders can flow around you.

Eat where locals queue and food is cooked to order. Be extra careful with ice, salads and shellfish in rural areas and the hot season; peel your own fruit.
In Phnom Penh, bag-snatching from passing motorbikes is the main risk: wear bags across the body on the side away from the road, and keep your phone out of sight near traffic.
Tap water is not safe to drink. Stick to sealed bottled or filtered water and check the seal. Outside the cities, ask for drinks without ice unless you are sure it is commercial ice.
Use Grab or the PassApp for tuk-tuks and cars, so the fare and route are logged.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled water is widely sold and refill stations exist in tourist towns. Outside the main towns, ask for no ice unless you know it is commercial.
Freshly grilled and boiled dishes from busy stalls are safest. Avoid raw or fermented meat/fish dishes such as laap dib — they carry a real parasite risk. Peel fruit yourself.
Laos is very relaxed and low-crime, but towns wind down early — plan transport before dark, especially in rural areas where lighting and taxis are scarce.
On tubing or river days around Vang Vieng, be careful with alcohol near fast water; this is the main cause of traveller injuries.

By far the most likely serious emergency a traveller faces in this region.
Get out of the traffic lane before anything else. Being hit a second time is a real risk on a fast road, and it is what turns a survivable crash into a fatal one.
Call the national emergency number. Say the road, the direction of travel and the nearest landmark or kilometre marker — a screenshot of your map pin is the fastest way to answer "where are you?".
Do not move anyone who has hit their head or complains of neck or back pain, unless leaving them is more dangerous than moving them.
Control heavy bleeding with firm, continuous pressure through whatever cloth you have. Keep pressing; do not lift to check.
Go to hospital even if you feel fine. Head injuries and internal bleeding declare themselves hours later, and road rash here infects fast in the heat.
Get a police report. Without one, most travel insurance and every vehicle claim is disputed. Ask for the report number before you leave.
Photograph everything at the scene: both vehicles, the road, the position, any licence and registration, and the other rider. Photographs settle later arguments that memory cannot.

Tell your insurer the same day. Many policies exclude motorcycle injury unless you hold a licence valid for that engine size and were wearing a helmet — know which before you rent, not after you crash.
Do not hand over your passport as security to a rental shop, a hospital or anyone at the scene. Offer a photocopy or a deposit instead — a withheld passport is the standard lever in a rental dispute.
Do not agree a cash settlement at the roadside before you know the extent of your own injuries.

Rare but not hypothetical — and methanol poisoning is survivable only if it is recognised early.
Treat sudden severe drunkenness that does not match how much was drunk as an emergency, especially after free shots, mixed spirits or home-made liquor.

Methanol poisoning classically appears 6–30 hours after drinking, not immediately: blurred or snowy vision, severe stomach pain, breathlessness, confusion. Any vision change after drinking spirits is a hospital emergency that night, not in the morning.
Get the person to the largest hospital you can reach and say the words "possible methanol poisoning". Treatment exists and works; delay is what kills.
If someone is unconscious but breathing, put them on their side so they cannot choke, and stay with them.
Keep the bottle, the glass or the receipt if you safely can — it helps the hospital and any investigation.
Report it to the tourist police and to your embassy. Clusters are how these venues get shut.
Do not let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a room. Almost every death in a spiking or methanol cluster involves someone left to sleep.
Do not accept drinks from a shared jug or a bucket you did not watch being poured, and do not leave a drink unattended.
Recoverable, but the order of the steps decides whether it takes two days or two weeks.
Report it to the local police and get a written report with a reference number. Every embassy asks for it, and so does your insurer.
Contact your embassy or consulate — the nearest one is usually in Bangkok, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City or Phnom Penh, and many countries have none at all in Laos.
If your visa or entry stamp was in it, immigration will need to reissue the record before you can leave the country. Start that on the same day.
Ask for an emergency travel document if you have a flight soon; a full replacement passport takes longer and may have to be issued from a regional hub.
Cancel and replace any cards that went with it, and change the passwords for anything that was unlocked on a stolen phone.
Do not leave the country by land while the entry record is unresolved — an unmatched entry stamp turns a lost passport into an immigration problem.
Do not rely on the photocopy alone. Keep a photograph of the data page and the entry stamp somewhere you can reach without your phone.

Snatch theft from a moving motorbike is the common version, and it injures people because they hold on.
Let it go. A bag is replaceable; being dragged along a road is how snatch theft causes serious injury and death.
If you are hurt, treat that first and go to hospital — the report can be made afterwards.
Report it to the tourist police where there is a tourist police unit; they usually have English speakers and handle traveller cases directly.
Freeze cards immediately and check for transactions — card cloning at ATMs is common in this region.
Get the written police report for your insurer; a verbal report is not enough for a claim.
Tell your embassy if a passport, a visa or your safety is involved.
Do not chase anyone, and do not confront a group.
Do not carry your only card, your only phone and your passport in the same bag.
Drug offences carry severe penalties across all four countries, including sentences travellers do not expect.
Ask immediately, clearly and repeatedly to contact your embassy. You are entitled to consular access; the request is what triggers it.
Do not sign anything you cannot read, and say so plainly. Ask for a translated copy and for a lawyer.
Stay calm and polite. Argument and raised voices make everything that follows harder.
The embassy can supply a list of local lawyers, contact your family and monitor your treatment.
Arrange money through family or your insurer rather than through anyone who approaches you at the station.
Do not offer money to a police officer. In a genuine arrest it converts a bad situation into a far worse one.
Do not assume a substance is legal because it is sold openly to tourists — cannabis law in Thailand has changed more than once and differs completely in the other three countries.
Drowning is the second leading cause of traveller death here, and rip currents cause most of it.
Caught in a rip: do not swim against it. Float, signal, and swim parallel to the beach until the pull stops, then come in at an angle.
Helping someone else: throw them something that floats and call for help. Swimming out to a panicking person is how one drowning becomes two.
Out of the water and not breathing: start chest compressions immediately — hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second — and send someone for an ambulance.
Anyone who has been under the water needs hospital assessment even if they seem fine afterwards.

For a jellyfish sting, flood the area with vinegar for at least thirty seconds and treat any breathing difficulty as an emergency. Box jellyfish are present in the Gulf of Thailand and around the Cambodian coast.
Do not swim where a red flag is flying, and do not judge a beach by how calm it looks — rips are strongest where the water appears flattest.
Do not drink and swim, and do not swim alone at night.

Dengue is the biggest infectious risk to travellers in this region, and it is seasonal rather than rare.
Any fever above 38 °C that lasts more than 24 hours needs a doctor and a blood test. Dengue, malaria and typhoid all start looking like flu.
Take paracetamol for fever and pain — nothing else.
Drink steadily. Dehydration is what turns a manageable dengue into an admission.
Warning signs that mean hospital now, not tomorrow: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, black stools, breathlessness, or a sudden drop in temperature with cold clammy skin.
Malaria is a risk in forested border areas rather than the cities. Tell the doctor exactly where you have been in the last month.
Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or any other anti-inflammatory until dengue has been ruled out — they increase bleeding risk.
Do not buy antimalarials or antibiotics from a small shop; counterfeit medicine is a genuine problem outside established pharmacies.
Common, usually self-limiting, and occasionally the thing that puts a traveller on a drip.
Rehydrate with oral rehydration salts, sold in every pharmacy in the region. Water alone does not replace what is being lost.
Small sips, often, are better tolerated than a glass at a time.
See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, a fever above 38.5 °C, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or symptoms lasting more than three days.
A young child, an older traveller or anyone pregnant should be seen much sooner than that.
Do not take a stop-the-symptoms antidiarrhoeal if there is blood or a high fever — it can make the underlying infection worse.
The regional hazards are seasonal flooding, tropical storms, and — on the Andaman coast — tsunami.

Feel a strong earthquake on the coast, or see the sea suddenly draw back? Move inland and uphill immediately and do not wait for an official warning. On the Andaman coast, follow the blue tsunami evacuation signs.
Flooding: never walk or drive through moving water. Thirty centimetres will float a car and knee-deep flow will take an adult off their feet. Flash floods in the northern gorges rise in minutes.
Storm: get indoors and away from windows, trees and hoardings. Boat services stop for a reason — do not press a captain to sail.
Assume the water is contaminated after any flood, and treat every cut and graze that touched it.
Register with your embassy’s travel service if one is available, so you can be contacted during a large event.
Do not rely on mobile coverage during a major event; agree a meeting point with anyone you are travelling with in advance.

Dengue is the biggest infectious risk to travellers in this region, and it is seasonal rather than rare.
Any fever above 38 °C that lasts more than 24 hours needs a doctor and a blood test. Dengue, malaria and typhoid all start looking like flu.
Take paracetamol for fever and pain — nothing else.
Drink steadily. Dehydration is what turns a manageable dengue into an admission.
Warning signs that mean hospital now, not tomorrow: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, black stools, breathlessness, or a sudden drop in temperature with cold clammy skin.
Malaria is a risk in forested border areas rather than the cities. Tell the doctor exactly where you have been in the last month.
Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or any other anti-inflammatory until dengue has been ruled out — they increase bleeding risk.
Do not buy antimalarials or antibiotics from a small shop; counterfeit medicine is a genuine problem outside established pharmacies.
Common, usually self-limiting, and occasionally the thing that puts a traveller on a drip.
Rehydrate with oral rehydration salts, sold in every pharmacy in the region. Water alone does not replace what is being lost.
Small sips, often, are better tolerated than a glass at a time.
See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, a fever above 38.5 °C, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or symptoms lasting more than three days.
A young child, an older traveller or anyone pregnant should be seen much sooner than that.
Do not take a stop-the-symptoms antidiarrhoeal if there is blood or a high fever — it can make the underlying infection worse.

Fire in a hotel or hostel
Older guesthouses across the region often have one staircase, barred windows and no working alarm.
Get out and stay out. Do not stop for luggage.
Stay low under smoke, and feel a door with the back of your hand before opening it.
If you cannot get out, close the door, block the gap with wet cloth, get to a window and make yourself visible.
Account for everyone you are travelling with at a point away from the building.
Do not use a lift. Check where the stairs are on the night you arrive — it takes ten seconds and it is the whole of fire safety in a strange building.
Someone you are travelling with is missing
Report it to the police immediately. There is no waiting period, and the first hours matter most.
Contact your embassy at the same time — they can press a case that a local station may otherwise treat as routine.
Check the hospitals in the area as well as the police; someone brought in unconscious and without documents may not be identified for a while.
Gather a recent photograph, what they were wearing, their phone number and any location-sharing they had switched on.
Ask their accommodation, their last known driver or boat operator, and the last place they were seen. Local businesses often know more than a station does.
Do not delay to "give it another day". The advice from every consular service is to report early and stand it down later if it was nothing.
Long trips, isolation, heat, drink and sleeplessness make this more common on the road than at home.
If someone is at immediate risk of harming themselves, do not leave them alone, and call the national emergency number.
Get to a hospital emergency department; the larger private hospitals in Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Phnom Penh have psychiatric services, most public provincial hospitals do not.
Remove the immediate means of harm if you can do so safely.
Your travel insurer’s assistance line can arrange a psychiatric referral and, where needed, a medically escorted flight home.
Your embassy can contact family and help with practical arrangements.
Local mental health services are limited in Cambodia and Laos in particular; getting to a major city, or home, is often the realistic plan.
Do not treat "they have been drinking" as an explanation that makes it less urgent.

After washing, apply an antiseptic such as povidone-iodine or 70% alcohol if you have it, and cover the wound loosely.
Auto-injectors are hard to buy in Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos and are often unavailable outside major private hospitals.
Bangkok’s BTS and MRT and the inter-city VIP buses and trains are reliable; on overnight trains you can request a lower berth when booking.

CPR and choking for every age, allergic reactions, bleeding, heart attack and stroke, a full babies-and-children section, snakes and marine life, and how to actually get help here. Checked against named medical authorities — see its own sources.

Checked hospitals with a 24-hour emergency department come first (children’s care first for a family), then straight-line distance. Closer places from OpenStreetMap follow, unchecked. The full screen has the rest of the country, what to do where nothing is listed, how people reach a hospital here, and your medical card.
Choose accommodation with strong recent reviews and 24-hour reception; a door that locks from the inside, and a padlock for hostel lockers, are worth it.

Consular help is free and is the right first call for a lost passport, an arrest, a death or a large-scale emergency. Find yours and save the address now — searching for it during the emergency is the part that goes wrong.
Do not apply a tight tourniquet, ice, alcohol or an electric shock.
Do not chase or try to kill the snake, and do not wait to “see if it was venomous”.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck out the venom.
Do not dismiss a minor scratch or a lick on broken skin — these can pass on rabies too.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled and filtered water is cheap and everywhere, with refill stations in most towns. Ice in cafés and restaurants is factory-made and generally safe.
Do not make them stand up or walk around.
Do not rub the area or rinse with fresh water — it can fire more stinging cells.
Do not scrub hard enough to bruise the tissue, and do not have the wound stitched closed straight away unless a doctor decides it is necessary — leave it open after washing.
Do not wait for symptoms to worsen before using adrenaline.
Do not wait to “see if the animal was sick”, and do not assume a calm or healthy-looking animal is safe.
Dress modestly at temples (shoulders and knees covered) and more conservatively in rural and Muslim-majority areas; it draws less attention and respects local custom.

For a stonefish or stingray wound, soak the area in water as hot as can be comfortably tolerated (around 45°C). A sea-urchin puncture is different: wash it with soap and water instead — do not use the hot-water method on that one.
Get out of the water. Douse the sting with vinegar for at least 30 seconds — many beaches keep a bottle for this.

Get to a clinic or hospital the same day for rabies post-exposure vaccination — do not wait for symptoms. Dog, cat, monkey and bat bites or scratches across this region can carry rabies, which is almost always fatal once symptoms begin but is nearly always preventable when treatment starts promptly.
Get to a hospital even if they improve — symptoms can return hours later.
Get to a hospital that can give antivenom as fast as possible, and call the emergency number on the way.
Honest guidance on adrenaline auto-injectors and defibrillators — neither is reliably bought on the street in this region — plus hands-only CPR.
If an adrenaline auto-injector (EpiPen) is available, use it at once into the outer thigh, then call emergency services.

If someone collapses and is not breathing normally, send someone to call the emergency number and fetch an AED, then start hands-only CPR: push hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second, until help arrives.
If you are at risk of anaphylaxis, bring at least two from home, carry them on your person (not in checked luggage) and keep them out of extreme heat.
If you were vaccinated against rabies before the trip, you still need booster doses after a bite — say so at the clinic.
Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint or sling.

In a serious emergency, call the number above. Show this screen to a local to ask for help. Tourist police often speak English. First-aid guidance here is general and does not replace professional medical care.
In an emergency, hospital emergency rooms and ambulances carry injectable adrenaline given by staff — reaching one fast matters more than finding a pharmacy.
Lay the person flat and raise their legs; if breathing is hard, let them sit up. A second dose may be needed after about 5 minutes if there is no improvement.
Lift off any tentacles with the edge of a card or a gloved hand.
Move out of the snake’s reach; keep the person calm and as still as possible — panic and movement speed venom through the body.
Note the snake’s colour, size and shape, or photograph it from a safe distance — it helps doctors choose the antivenom.
On the islands, take care at Full Moon-style parties: go with people you trust, mind your drink, and arrange your return boat or taxi in advance.
Public AEDs are not widely mapped in the region. You are most likely to find one at international airports, large shopping malls, five-star hotels and hospitals — ask staff or security.
Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts.
Rent a scooter only with the correct licence and a helmet — road injuries are the single biggest real risk to travellers here.
Show or speak these to hospital staff or anyone helping you. Works offline.
Show “I need a hospital” to a local (works offline)
Signs: swelling of the lips, tongue or throat, trouble breathing, widespread hives, or dizziness or collapse after a sting, food or medicine.
Street food is a highlight and safe when the stall is busy and food is cooked fresh in front of you. Peel your own fruit, and be cautious with reheated buffet dishes left standing.
Tap the one that fits. Each opens what to do in the next minute, what to do in the next few hours, and the mistake people reliably make. Works offline.
Tell the clinic if the skin was broken, if a bat was involved, or if saliva reached your eyes, mouth or an open cut — these also need rabies immunoglobulin, not the vaccine alone.

Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos are, by global standards, among the safer places to travel solo — including for women. Ordinary city precautions apply; violent crime against tourists is rare and opportunistic theft is the main risk.
To try to buy one locally, ask the pharmacy of a large international hospital (for example Bumrungrad or Samitivej in Bangkok). Availability is not guaranteed — telephone ahead.
Treat any difficulty breathing, chest pain or collapse as life-threatening, start CPR if needed, and call for help — box jellyfish stings can kill within minutes.
Trust your instincts — it is always fine to be firm, say no, or walk away. Save the tourist-police and your embassy numbers offline before you need them.
Use booked ride apps (Grab, Bolt) or metered taxis rather than unmarked cars, especially at night, and check the plate before getting in. Share your live trip with someone you trust.

Wash the wound at once with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes — thorough washing alone removes much of the virus and is the single most important step. If there is no soap, flush with plenty of water.
Watch your drink at bars and parties — drink-spiking happens at some nightlife spots. Keep enough phone charge and a little cash for a ride home.
What to do first — then get to a hospital. General first aid, not a substitute for a doctor.
Eat where locals queue and food is cooked to order. Be extra careful with ice, salads and shellfish in rural areas and the hot season; peel your own fruit.
In Phnom Penh, bag-snatching from passing motorbikes is the main risk: wear bags across the body on the side away from the road, and keep your phone out of sight near traffic.
Tap water is not safe to drink. Stick to sealed bottled or filtered water and check the seal. Outside the cities, ask for drinks without ice unless you are sure it is commercial ice.
Use Grab or the PassApp for tuk-tuks and cars, so the fare and route are logged.
Do not drink the tap water. Bottled water is widely sold and refill stations exist in tourist towns. Outside the main towns, ask for no ice unless you know it is commercial.
Freshly grilled and boiled dishes from busy stalls are safest. Avoid raw or fermented meat/fish dishes such as laap dib — they carry a real parasite risk. Peel fruit yourself.
Laos is very relaxed and low-crime, but towns wind down early — plan transport before dark, especially in rural areas where lighting and taxis are scarce.
On tubing or river days around Vang Vieng, be careful with alcohol near fast water; this is the main cause of traveller injuries.
Busy stalls with high turnover are safest — choose freshly cooked, steaming dishes. Go easy on raw herbs you cannot wash yourself and on shellfish in hot weather.
Carry bags on the pavement side and keep phones away from the kerb; snatch-thefts from passing motorbikes happen in Ho Chi Minh City and Hanoi.

By far the most likely serious emergency a traveller faces in this region.
Get out of the traffic lane before anything else. Being hit a second time is a real risk on a fast road, and it is what turns a survivable crash into a fatal one.
Call the national emergency number. Say the road, the direction of travel and the nearest landmark or kilometre marker — a screenshot of your map pin is the fastest way to answer "where are you?".
Do not move anyone who has hit their head or complains of neck or back pain, unless leaving them is more dangerous than moving them.
Control heavy bleeding with firm, continuous pressure through whatever cloth you have. Keep pressing; do not lift to check.
Go to hospital even if you feel fine. Head injuries and internal bleeding declare themselves hours later, and road rash here infects fast in the heat.
Get a police report. Without one, most travel insurance and every vehicle claim is disputed. Ask for the report number before you leave.
Photograph everything at the scene: both vehicles, the road, the position, any licence and registration, and the other rider. Photographs settle later arguments that memory cannot.

Tell your insurer the same day. Many policies exclude motorcycle injury unless you hold a licence valid for that engine size and were wearing a helmet — know which before you rent, not after you crash.
Do not hand over your passport as security to a rental shop, a hospital or anyone at the scene. Offer a photocopy or a deposit instead — a withheld passport is the standard lever in a rental dispute.
Do not agree a cash settlement at the roadside before you know the extent of your own injuries.
Rare but not hypothetical — and methanol poisoning is survivable only if it is recognised early.
Treat sudden severe drunkenness that does not match how much was drunk as an emergency, especially after free shots, mixed spirits or home-made liquor.

Methanol poisoning classically appears 6–30 hours after drinking, not immediately: blurred or snowy vision, severe stomach pain, breathlessness, confusion. Any vision change after drinking spirits is a hospital emergency that night, not in the morning.
Get the person to the largest hospital you can reach and say the words "possible methanol poisoning". Treatment exists and works; delay is what kills.
If someone is unconscious but breathing, put them on their side so they cannot choke, and stay with them.
Keep the bottle, the glass or the receipt if you safely can — it helps the hospital and any investigation.
Report it to the tourist police and to your embassy. Clusters are how these venues get shut.
Do not let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a room. Almost every death in a spiking or methanol cluster involves someone left to sleep.
Do not accept drinks from a shared jug or a bucket you did not watch being poured, and do not leave a drink unattended.
Recoverable, but the order of the steps decides whether it takes two days or two weeks.
Report it to the local police and get a written report with a reference number. Every embassy asks for it, and so does your insurer.
Contact your embassy or consulate — the nearest one is usually in Bangkok, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City or Phnom Penh, and many countries have none at all in Laos.
If your visa or entry stamp was in it, immigration will need to reissue the record before you can leave the country. Start that on the same day.
Ask for an emergency travel document if you have a flight soon; a full replacement passport takes longer and may have to be issued from a regional hub.
Cancel and replace any cards that went with it, and change the passwords for anything that was unlocked on a stolen phone.
Do not leave the country by land while the entry record is unresolved — an unmatched entry stamp turns a lost passport into an immigration problem.
Do not rely on the photocopy alone. Keep a photograph of the data page and the entry stamp somewhere you can reach without your phone.
Snatch theft from a moving motorbike is the common version, and it injures people because they hold on.
Let it go. A bag is replaceable; being dragged along a road is how snatch theft causes serious injury and death.
If you are hurt, treat that first and go to hospital — the report can be made afterwards.
Report it to the tourist police where there is a tourist police unit; they usually have English speakers and handle traveller cases directly.
Freeze cards immediately and check for transactions — card cloning at ATMs is common in this region.
Get the written police report for your insurer; a verbal report is not enough for a claim.
Tell your embassy if a passport, a visa or your safety is involved.
Do not chase anyone, and do not confront a group.
Do not carry your only card, your only phone and your passport in the same bag.
Drug offences carry severe penalties across all four countries, including sentences travellers do not expect.
Ask immediately, clearly and repeatedly to contact your embassy. You are entitled to consular access; the request is what triggers it.
Do not sign anything you cannot read, and say so plainly. Ask for a translated copy and for a lawyer.
Stay calm and polite. Argument and raised voices make everything that follows harder.
The embassy can supply a list of local lawyers, contact your family and monitor your treatment.
Arrange money through family or your insurer rather than through anyone who approaches you at the station.
Do not offer money to a police officer. In a genuine arrest it converts a bad situation into a far worse one.
Do not assume a substance is legal because it is sold openly to tourists — cannabis law in Thailand has changed more than once and differs completely in the other three countries.
Drowning is the second leading cause of traveller death here, and rip currents cause most of it.
Caught in a rip: do not swim against it. Float, signal, and swim parallel to the beach until the pull stops, then come in at an angle.
Helping someone else: throw them something that floats and call for help. Swimming out to a panicking person is how one drowning becomes two.
Out of the water and not breathing: start chest compressions immediately — hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second — and send someone for an ambulance.
Anyone who has been under the water needs hospital assessment even if they seem fine afterwards.

For a jellyfish sting, flood the area with vinegar for at least thirty seconds and treat any breathing difficulty as an emergency. Box jellyfish are present in the Gulf of Thailand and around the Cambodian coast.
Do not swim where a red flag is flying, and do not judge a beach by how calm it looks — rips are strongest where the water appears flattest.
Do not drink and swim, and do not swim alone at night.
Dengue is the biggest infectious risk to travellers in this region, and it is seasonal rather than rare.
Any fever above 38 °C that lasts more than 24 hours needs a doctor and a blood test. Dengue, malaria and typhoid all start looking like flu.
Take paracetamol for fever and pain — nothing else.
Drink steadily. Dehydration is what turns a manageable dengue into an admission.
Warning signs that mean hospital now, not tomorrow: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, black stools, breathlessness, or a sudden drop in temperature with cold clammy skin.
Malaria is a risk in forested border areas rather than the cities. Tell the doctor exactly where you have been in the last month.
Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or any other anti-inflammatory until dengue has been ruled out — they increase bleeding risk.
Do not buy antimalarials or antibiotics from a small shop; counterfeit medicine is a genuine problem outside established pharmacies.
Common, usually self-limiting, and occasionally the thing that puts a traveller on a drip.
Rehydrate with oral rehydration salts, sold in every pharmacy in the region. Water alone does not replace what is being lost.
Small sips, often, are better tolerated than a glass at a time.
See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, a fever above 38.5 °C, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or symptoms lasting more than three days.
A young child, an older traveller or anyone pregnant should be seen much sooner than that.
Do not take a stop-the-symptoms antidiarrhoeal if there is blood or a high fever — it can make the underlying infection worse.
The regional hazards are seasonal flooding, tropical storms, and — on the Andaman coast — tsunami.

Feel a strong earthquake on the coast, or see the sea suddenly draw back? Move inland and uphill immediately and do not wait for an official warning. On the Andaman coast, follow the blue tsunami evacuation signs.
Flooding: never walk or drive through moving water. Thirty centimetres will float a car and knee-deep flow will take an adult off their feet. Flash floods in the northern gorges rise in minutes.
Storm: get indoors and away from windows, trees and hoardings. Boat services stop for a reason — do not press a captain to sail.
Assume the water is contaminated after any flood, and treat every cut and graze that touched it.
Register with your embassy’s travel service if one is available, so you can be contacted during a large event.
Do not rely on mobile coverage during a major event; agree a meeting point with anyone you are travelling with in advance.
Fire in a hotel or hostel
Older guesthouses across the region often have one staircase, barred windows and no working alarm.
Get out and stay out. Do not stop for luggage.
Stay low under smoke, and feel a door with the back of your hand before opening it.
If you cannot get out, close the door, block the gap with wet cloth, get to a window and make yourself visible.
Account for everyone you are travelling with at a point away from the building.
Do not use a lift. Check where the stairs are on the night you arrive — it takes ten seconds and it is the whole of fire safety in a strange building.
Someone you are travelling with is missing
Report it to the police immediately. There is no waiting period, and the first hours matter most.
Contact your embassy at the same time — they can press a case that a local station may otherwise treat as routine.
Check the hospitals in the area as well as the police; someone brought in unconscious and without documents may not be identified for a while.
Gather a recent photograph, what they were wearing, their phone number and any location-sharing they had switched on.
Ask their accommodation, their last known driver or boat operator, and the last place they were seen. Local businesses often know more than a station does.
Do not delay to "give it another day". The advice from every consular service is to report early and stand it down later if it was nothing.
Long trips, isolation, heat, drink and sleeplessness make this more common on the road than at home.
If someone is at immediate risk of harming themselves, do not leave them alone, and call the national emergency number.
Get to a hospital emergency department; the larger private hospitals in Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Phnom Penh have psychiatric services, most public provincial hospitals do not.
Remove the immediate means of harm if you can do so safely.
Your travel insurer’s assistance line can arrange a psychiatric referral and, where needed, a medically escorted flight home.
Your embassy can contact family and help with practical arrangements.
Local mental health services are limited in Cambodia and Laos in particular; getting to a major city, or home, is often the realistic plan.
Do not treat "they have been drinking" as an explanation that makes it less urgent.
The hardest page here, written down so nobody has to work it out while grieving.
Contact your embassy or consulate first. Repatriation, local registration of the death and the paperwork all run through them, and they will explain the order of it.
Contact the travel insurer. Repatriation of remains is expensive and is the single most valuable thing a policy covers.
A local death certificate is issued by the authorities where the death occurred; the embassy can advise on getting it recognised at home.
Do not agree to a cremation or a burial before speaking to the embassy and the family — in some countries it cannot be undone or reversed.
Issue an emergency travel document or a replacement passport.
Contact your family and help you get money sent to you.
Visit you and monitor your treatment if you are arrested or detained.
Give you a list of local lawyers, translators and doctors.
Help in a death, a serious accident, or a large-scale emergency.
Give you the current official travel and health advice for where you are.
Get you out of prison, or interfere in a local investigation or court case.
Pay your medical bills, your legal costs or your fare home.
Investigate a crime, or make the police act faster than local law allows.
Give you legal or medical advice of its own.

Many countries have an embassy in Bangkok, Hanoi and Phnom Penh but none at all in Vientiane — in Laos your nearest consular help is often in Bangkok. Find yours, and save the address and the emergency line, before you need it.
By far the most likely serious emergency a traveller faces in this region.
Get out of the traffic lane before anything else. Being hit a second time is a real risk on a fast road, and it is what turns a survivable crash into a fatal one.
Call the national emergency number. Say the road, the direction of travel and the nearest landmark or kilometre marker — a screenshot of your map pin is the fastest way to answer "where are you?".
Do not move anyone who has hit their head or complains of neck or back pain, unless leaving them is more dangerous than moving them.
Control heavy bleeding with firm, continuous pressure through whatever cloth you have. Keep pressing; do not lift to check.
Go to hospital even if you feel fine. Head injuries and internal bleeding declare themselves hours later, and road rash here infects fast in the heat.
Get a police report. Without one, most travel insurance and every vehicle claim is disputed. Ask for the report number before you leave.
Photograph everything at the scene: both vehicles, the road, the position, any licence and registration, and the other rider. Photographs settle later arguments that memory cannot.

Tell your insurer the same day. Many policies exclude motorcycle injury unless you hold a licence valid for that engine size and were wearing a helmet — know which before you rent, not after you crash.
Do not hand over your passport as security to a rental shop, a hospital or anyone at the scene. Offer a photocopy or a deposit instead — a withheld passport is the standard lever in a rental dispute.
Do not agree a cash settlement at the roadside before you know the extent of your own injuries.
Rare but not hypothetical — and methanol poisoning is survivable only if it is recognised early.
Treat sudden severe drunkenness that does not match how much was drunk as an emergency, especially after free shots, mixed spirits or home-made liquor.

Get the person to the largest hospital you can reach and say the words "possible methanol poisoning". Treatment exists and works; delay is what kills.
If someone is unconscious but breathing, put them on their side so they cannot choke, and stay with them.
Keep the bottle, the glass or the receipt if you safely can — it helps the hospital and any investigation.
Report it to the tourist police and to your embassy. Clusters are how these venues get shut.
Do not let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a room. Almost every death in a spiking or methanol cluster involves someone left to sleep.
Do not accept drinks from a shared jug or a bucket you did not watch being poured, and do not leave a drink unattended.

If your visa or entry stamp was in it, immigration will need to reissue the record before you can leave the country. Start that on the same day.
Ask for an emergency travel document if you have a flight soon; a full replacement passport takes longer and may have to be issued from a regional hub.
Cancel and replace any cards that went with it, and change the passwords for anything that was unlocked on a stolen phone.

Let it go. A bag is replaceable; being dragged along a road is how snatch theft causes serious injury and death.

If someone is unconscious but breathing, put them on their side so they cannot choke, and stay with them.
Keep the bottle, the glass or the receipt if you safely can — it helps the hospital and any investigation.
Report it to the tourist police and to your embassy. Clusters are how these venues get shut.
Do not let anyone "sleep it off" alone in a room. Almost every death in a spiking or methanol cluster involves someone left to sleep.
Do not accept drinks from a shared jug or a bucket you did not watch being poured, and do not leave a drink unattended.
Recoverable, but the order of the steps decides whether it takes two days or two weeks.
Report it to the local police and get a written report with a reference number. Every embassy asks for it, and so does your insurer.
Contact your embassy or consulate — the nearest one is usually in Bangkok, Hanoi, Ho Chi Minh City or Phnom Penh, and many countries have none at all in Laos.
If your visa or entry stamp was in it, immigration will need to reissue the record before you can leave the country. Start that on the same day.
Ask for an emergency travel document if you have a flight soon; a full replacement passport takes longer and may have to be issued from a regional hub.
Cancel and replace any cards that went with it, and change the passwords for anything that was unlocked on a stolen phone.
Do not leave the country by land while the entry record is unresolved — an unmatched entry stamp turns a lost passport into an immigration problem.
Do not rely on the photocopy alone. Keep a photograph of the data page and the entry stamp somewhere you can reach without your phone.
Snatch theft from a moving motorbike is the common version, and it injures people because they hold on.
Let it go. A bag is replaceable; being dragged along a road is how snatch theft causes serious injury and death.
If you are hurt, treat that first and go to hospital — the report can be made afterwards.
Report it to the tourist police where there is a tourist police unit; they usually have English speakers and handle traveller cases directly.
Freeze cards immediately and check for transactions — card cloning at ATMs is common in this region.
Get the written police report for your insurer; a verbal report is not enough for a claim.
Tell your embassy if a passport, a visa or your safety is involved.
Do not chase anyone, and do not confront a group.
Do not carry your only card, your only phone and your passport in the same bag.
Drug offences carry severe penalties across all four countries, including sentences travellers do not expect.
Ask immediately, clearly and repeatedly to contact your embassy. You are entitled to consular access; the request is what triggers it.
Do not sign anything you cannot read, and say so plainly. Ask for a translated copy and for a lawyer.
Stay calm and polite. Argument and raised voices make everything that follows harder.
The embassy can supply a list of local lawyers, contact your family and monitor your treatment.
Arrange money through family or your insurer rather than through anyone who approaches you at the station.
Do not offer money to a police officer. In a genuine arrest it converts a bad situation into a far worse one.
Do not assume a substance is legal because it is sold openly to tourists — cannabis law in Thailand has changed more than once and differs completely in the other three countries.
Drowning is the second leading cause of traveller death here, and rip currents cause most of it.
Caught in a rip: do not swim against it. Float, signal, and swim parallel to the beach until the pull stops, then come in at an angle.
Helping someone else: throw them something that floats and call for help. Swimming out to a panicking person is how one drowning becomes two.
Out of the water and not breathing: start chest compressions immediately — hard and fast in the centre of the chest, about twice a second — and send someone for an ambulance.
Anyone who has been under the water needs hospital assessment even if they seem fine afterwards.

For a jellyfish sting, flood the area with vinegar for at least thirty seconds and treat any breathing difficulty as an emergency. Box jellyfish are present in the Gulf of Thailand and around the Cambodian coast.
Do not swim where a red flag is flying, and do not judge a beach by how calm it looks — rips are strongest where the water appears flattest.
Do not drink and swim, and do not swim alone at night.
Dengue is the biggest infectious risk to travellers in this region, and it is seasonal rather than rare.
Any fever above 38 °C that lasts more than 24 hours needs a doctor and a blood test. Dengue, malaria and typhoid all start looking like flu.
Take paracetamol for fever and pain — nothing else.
Drink steadily. Dehydration is what turns a manageable dengue into an admission.
Warning signs that mean hospital now, not tomorrow: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, bleeding gums or nose, black stools, breathlessness, or a sudden drop in temperature with cold clammy skin.
Malaria is a risk in forested border areas rather than the cities. Tell the doctor exactly where you have been in the last month.
Do not take ibuprofen, aspirin or any other anti-inflammatory until dengue has been ruled out — they increase bleeding risk.
Do not buy antimalarials or antibiotics from a small shop; counterfeit medicine is a genuine problem outside established pharmacies.
Common, usually self-limiting, and occasionally the thing that puts a traveller on a drip.
Rehydrate with oral rehydration salts, sold in every pharmacy in the region. Water alone does not replace what is being lost.
Small sips, often, are better tolerated than a glass at a time.
See a doctor if there is blood in the stool, a fever above 38.5 °C, vomiting that stops you keeping fluids down, or symptoms lasting more than three days.
A young child, an older traveller or anyone pregnant should be seen much sooner than that.
Do not take a stop-the-symptoms antidiarrhoeal if there is blood or a high fever — it can make the underlying infection worse.
The regional hazards are seasonal flooding, tropical storms, and — on the Andaman coast — tsunami.

Feel a strong earthquake on the coast, or see the sea suddenly draw back? Move inland and uphill immediately and do not wait for an official warning. On the Andaman coast, follow the blue tsunami evacuation signs.
Flooding: never walk or drive through moving water. Thirty centimetres will float a car and knee-deep flow will take an adult off their feet. Flash floods in the northern gorges rise in minutes.
Storm: get indoors and away from windows, trees and hoardings. Boat services stop for a reason — do not press a captain to sail.
Assume the water is contaminated after any flood, and treat every cut and graze that touched it.
Register with your embassy’s travel service if one is available, so you can be contacted during a large event.
Do not rely on mobile coverage during a major event; agree a meeting point with anyone you are travelling with in advance.
Fire in a hotel or hostel
Older guesthouses across the region often have one staircase, barred windows and no working alarm.
Get out and stay out. Do not stop for luggage.
Stay low under smoke, and feel a door with the back of your hand before opening it.
If you cannot get out, close the door, block the gap with wet cloth, get to a window and make yourself visible.
Account for everyone you are travelling with at a point away from the building.
Do not use a lift. Check where the stairs are on the night you arrive — it takes ten seconds and it is the whole of fire safety in a strange building.
Someone you are travelling with is missing
Report it to the police immediately. There is no waiting period, and the first hours matter most.
Contact your embassy at the same time — they can press a case that a local station may otherwise treat as routine.
Check the hospitals in the area as well as the police; someone brought in unconscious and without documents may not be identified for a while.
Gather a recent photograph, what they were wearing, their phone number and any location-sharing they had switched on.
Ask their accommodation, their last known driver or boat operator, and the last place they were seen. Local businesses often know more than a station does.
Do not delay to "give it another day". The advice from every consular service is to report early and stand it down later if it was nothing.
Long trips, isolation, heat, drink and sleeplessness make this more common on the road than at home.
If someone is at immediate risk of harming themselves, do not leave them alone, and call the national emergency number.
Get to a hospital emergency department; the larger private hospitals in Bangkok, Ho Chi Minh City, Hanoi and Phnom Penh have psychiatric services, most public provincial hospitals do not.
Remove the immediate means of harm if you can do so safely.
Your travel insurer’s assistance line can arrange a psychiatric referral and, where needed, a medically escorted flight home.
Your embassy can contact family and help with practical arrangements.
Local mental health services are limited in Cambodia and Laos in particular; getting to a major city, or home, is often the realistic plan.
Do not treat "they have been drinking" as an explanation that makes it less urgent.
The hardest page here, written down so nobody has to work it out while grieving.
Contact your embassy or consulate first. Repatriation, local registration of the death and the paperwork all run through them, and they will explain the order of it.
Contact the travel insurer. Repatriation of remains is expensive and is the single most valuable thing a policy covers.
A local death certificate is issued by the authorities where the death occurred; the embassy can advise on getting it recognised at home.
Do not agree to a cremation or a burial before speaking to the embassy and the family — in some countries it cannot be undone or reversed.
Issue an emergency travel document or a replacement passport.
Contact your family and help you get money sent to you.
Visit you and monitor your treatment if you are arrested or detained.
Give you a list of local lawyers, translators and doctors.
Help in a death, a serious accident, or a large-scale emergency.
Give you the current official travel and health advice for where you are.
Get you out of prison, or interfere in a local investigation or court case.
Pay your medical bills, your legal costs or your fare home.
Investigate a crime, or make the police act faster than local law allows.
Give you legal or medical advice of its own.

Many countries have an embassy in Bangkok, Hanoi and Phnom Penh but none at all in Vientiane — in Laos your nearest consular help is often in Bangkok. Find yours, and save the address and the emergency line, before you need it.

Not responding, or not breathing normally
Someone collapses, or will not wake up
Check for a response — speak loudly and gently shake their shoulders (a baby: tap the foot, do not shake).
If they respond and are breathing normally: do not move them if you suspect a neck or back injury; otherwise put them in the recovery position (below) and keep checking their breathing.
If they do NOT respond: shout for help, and check breathing for up to 10 seconds — look, listen, feel. Noisy, gasping or irregular breathing counts as "not breathing normally".

Not breathing, or not breathing normally: call the emergency number on speakerphone (or send someone to) and start CPR immediately — see the adult/child or baby steps below. Do not wait to find a pulse; lay rescuers are not asked to check for one.
Send someone to find an AED (defibrillator) if one might be nearby — large hotels, malls and airports sometimes have one.
CPR — adult and child over about 1 year
Lay them on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone); for a child, one or two hands depending on their size.
Push hard and fast: adult depth 5–6 cm, child about one-third of the chest’s depth (roughly 5 cm) — both at 100–120 pushes per minute, letting the chest fully rise between pushes.

If trained and willing: 30 pushes, then 2 rescue breaths, repeating (children may be given 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers). If untrained, unwilling, or unable to give breaths: continuous push-only CPR is still far better than nothing.
Use an AED the moment one arrives and follow its voice prompts — it will not shock unless a shock is needed.
Keep going until the person starts breathing normally, professional help takes over, or you are physically unable to continue.

Alone with no phone: with an adult, call first, then start CPR. With a child, current guidance is to give CPR for about one to two minutes first if you truly cannot call and compress at the same time (put the phone on speaker and start compressions the moment you have dialled, if that is possible instead).

A rescuer taught with breaths first (5 initial breaths before compressions, still taught in the UK/Europe for children) and one taught compressions-first (the US/AHA approach) are both following a currently-endorsed method — do not hesitate over which to use.
Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface, head in a neutral position (not tilted back).
For rescue breaths, your mouth covers the baby’s mouth AND nose.

Compress the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line, using two thumbs wrapped around the chest (preferred where you can manage it) or the heel of one hand if you cannot encircle the chest — two fingers is also still taught in some countries and is not wrong if that is what you learned.
Push at least one-third of the chest’s depth (about 4 cm), 100–120 per minute.
30 compressions to 2 breaths for a single rescuer; 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers.
Keep going until the baby responds, help takes over, or you cannot continue.

Which hand technique is "correct" is genuinely still shifting between countries as of 2026 — two-thumb encircling is now preferred almost everywhere, but two-finger and heel-of-one-hand are still taught and are not mistakes.

Choking — adult and child over about 1 year
If they can cough, speak or breathe: encourage coughing and do nothing else yet.
If they cannot cough, speak or breathe: give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

Not cleared: give up to 5 abdominal thrusts — stand behind them, fist just above the navel, pull sharply inward and upward. (Some countries — Australia and New Zealand — teach chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts; both are recognised as effective.)
Keep alternating 5 back blows with 5 thrusts until the object clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
If they become unresponsive: lower them to the ground and start CPR (above) — look in the mouth each time you open the airway and only remove an object you can actually see.
Anyone who was given abdominal thrusts should see a doctor afterwards, even once the object is out — they can cause internal injury.
Never do a blind finger sweep of the mouth.
Lay the baby face down along your forearm or thigh, head lower than their chest, supporting the head and jaw.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking between each.

Not cleared: turn the baby face up (still head-down along your arm/thigh) and give up to 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line — two fingers, two thumbs, or the heel of one hand are all currently taught; use whichever you know.
Keep alternating 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts.
If the baby becomes unresponsive: start baby CPR (above) and get emergency help.
Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby — real risk of internal injury.
Never do a blind finger sweep; only remove an object you can actually see.

For someone unresponsive but breathing normally, with no reason to suspect CPR or serious bleeding is needed: roll them onto their side and tilt the head back slightly, so the airway stays open and fluid can drain out. Do not put them on their back.
A baby: do not put them on the floor — hold them face down along your forearm, head supported and tilted a little lower than the body.
Keep watching their breathing until help arrives. Noisy, irregular or gasping breathing is a sign to treat them as not breathing and start CPR instead.
A pregnant woman should go on her LEFT side.
Do not swim out to them unless you are trained for water rescue — reach with a pole, branch or rope, or throw something that floats, instead.

Once they are out of the water and not breathing normally: open the airway and give a few rescue breaths (guidance ranges from 2 to 5; 5 is now the most common number taught), then continue CPR at the normal ratio (30 compressions to 2 breaths).

Untrained, unwilling or unable to give breaths: compression-only CPR is still far better than nothing, but breaths genuinely improve survival after drowning specifically, more than in an ordinary adult cardiac arrest — give them if you can.
Vomiting is common during resuscitation — be ready to roll the person onto their side and clear the mouth, then continue.

Everyone who was pulled from the water unresponsive, needed rescue breaths or CPR, or has any cough, breathlessness, confusion or drowsiness afterwards must be seen at a hospital, even if they seem to recover — a delayed reaction (secondary drowning) is real.

Use their own prescribed auto-injector at its prescribed dose the moment anaphylaxis is suspected.
Auto-injector doses run roughly: 0.1 mg for about 7.5–15 kg (where that device exists), 0.15 mg from about 7.5–20 kg up to 30 kg depending on country and device, 0.3 mg above about 20–30 kg.
Under about 7.5 kg, or any child with no prescribed device: call the emergency number immediately and let paramedics or a doctor decide the dose — do not improvise with a mismatched adult device.
Dosing bands genuinely differ between countries and auto-injector brands — this is not a single fixed number worldwide. Always follow the child’s own prescribed device and plan where one exists.
Help them sit upright — never lie them down. Stay calm; anxiety worsens breathing.
Use the blue/grey reliever inhaler at once, with a spacer if one is available.
They have their own written asthma action plan: follow its dosing exactly.

No plan: either recognised approach is safe — 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs (UK-style), or 4 puffs (one at a time via a spacer, 4 breaths each), wait 4 minutes, then repeat (Australia-style).

Call the emergency number if: there is no inhaler, the inhaler is not helping, lips or fingers turn blue, the person is exhausted or confused, breathing becomes quiet or slow, or symptoms have not resolved after the full first round.
Apply firm, continuous direct pressure over the wound with whatever is available — a cloth, clothing, your hand.

Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: apply a tourniquet a few centimetres above the wound — never over a joint — and tighten until the bleeding stops. Note the exact time it went on and do not loosen it.

A proper manufactured tourniquet is best; sources genuinely disagree on improvising one from a belt or scarf as a last resort — most say it is better than nothing for life-threatening limb bleeding, one major source (Mayo Clinic) advises against it. If a limb is bleeding life-threateningly and nothing manufactured exists, an improvised tourniquet — a firm, wide band tightened with a rigid object — is the safer choice for most authorities.
Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing, confusion or weakness.
Treat the visible cause (e.g. control any bleeding).
Lie the person down; raise their legs if there is no injury (a leg fracture or suspected spinal injury) that raising them would make worse.
Keep them warm, loosen tight clothing, give nothing to eat or drink.
Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible — still worth doing up to about 3 hours after the burn.
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with cling film (not wrapped tightly around a limb) or a clean, non-fluffy dressing.
Chemical burn: flush continuously with plenty of water.
See a doctor for: a burn larger than the person’s palm; on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a major joint; any blistering burn in a baby or young child; or any electrical or chemical burn.
No ice, butter, toothpaste, creams or oils.
Heat stroke — confusion, agitation, drowsiness, collapse, hot skin that has STOPPED sweating, seizures: this is a medical emergency. Call for help and start cooling immediately.
Whole-body cold-water immersion (up to the neck) is the fastest method if available. If not: pour or soak with cold water and fan the person, with ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin.
Do not give anything to drink if the person is confused or not fully alert.
Heat exhaustion (milder — heavy sweating, tiredness, headache, nausea, still alert): move to shade, cool the skin, sip water or an oral rehydration/sports drink.
Protect them from injury — move hazards away; do not move the person unless they are somewhere dangerous.
Cushion the head; do not restrain them; put nothing in the mouth.
Once the jerking stops, place them in the recovery position (above).
Call the emergency number if: it lasts longer than 5 minutes, it repeats, it is their first ever seizure, they are injured, in water, pregnant, diabetic, or not waking up afterwards.
Febrile seizures in young children: same basic first aid — never put the child in a cold bath or undress them to bring a fever down.
Head or neck injury, road crash
Do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger. Keep the head and neck as still as possible.
A motorcycle helmet: leave it on unless you need to remove it to clear the airway or because they are not breathing.

Get to hospital for: repeated vomiting, increasing drowsiness or confusion, a worsening or persistent severe headache, a seizure, clear or blood-stained fluid from the nose or ears, or unequal pupil size.
Call the emergency number — do not delay this to find aspirin or for any other reason.
Help the person sit down and rest in a comfortable position.

If they are not allergic to aspirin, have no bleeding disorder, and have not already taken a full dose: have them chew an aspirin while waiting for help (chew a dose in the 150–500 mg range — 300 mg is standard in the UK, 162–325 mg in the US).
F — Face: has one side dropped?
A — Arms: can they raise both, or does one drift down?
S — Speech: is it slurred, or can they not speak?
T — Time: if any of these, call the emergency number immediately and note the exact time symptoms started — treatment is time-critical.
(Some guidance uses "BE FAST", adding Balance and Eyes — a strokes affecting balance or vision can be missed by the classic FAST test alone.)
Give nothing by mouth — food, drink or medicine — until swallowing has been medically checked.
Conscious and able to swallow: give 15–20 g of fast-acting sugar — glucose tablets, a sugary (not diet) drink, or sweets.
Recheck after 10–15 minutes and repeat if still low; once recovered, follow with a slower-acting snack.

Drowsy, confused or unconscious: give nothing by mouth (choking risk), put them in the recovery position, and call the emergency number. Give glucagon if one is available and you are trained to use it.
Call the emergency number for any severe bleeding.

Get to a clinic or hospital THE SAME DAY for rabies post-exposure treatment — do not wait to see if the animal seems sick. Vaccine (and immunoglobulin, where indicated) is available at provincial and most district hospitals in Thailand.
Vaccinated before the trip: you still need booster doses after a real exposure — say so at the clinic; you will need fewer doses and no immunoglobulin.
Dogs, cats, monkeys and bats can all carry rabies across Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos. A lick on broken skin is treated the same as a bite or scratch.
Do not try to swim straight back to shore against it — you will exhaust yourself.
Stay calm, float or tread water, and raise an arm and call out to signal for help.
Swim parallel to the shore to escape the current, or let it carry you out until it weakens (usually just past the breaking waves) and then swim back at an angle.

A red flag means do not swim. Thailand’s south-west monsoon (roughly May–October) brings rough seas and dangerous rip currents, especially on Andaman (west) coast beaches — ferries and speedboats, including those serving the Trat islands, are sometimes suspended in rough weather.
Hearing thunder or seeing lightning nearby: get indoors into a substantial building, or into a hard-topped (metal-roof) vehicle with the windows up.
Get out of the water and off the beach at once — do not shelter under a beach pavilion, umbrella or open-sided shelter.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunderclap before going back outside.
A lightning-strike victim carries no electrical charge — it is safe to touch them immediately and start CPR if they are not breathing.
Calling for help in Thailand — beyond the main number

1669 (medical emergency/ambulance) is free from any phone, works nationwide 24 hours, and operators can usually handle basic English — say "English" as soon as the call connects. Response is markedly slower on islands and in rural areas than in Bangkok.
191 is police, 199 is fire — both free and 24 hours.
1155 is the Tourist Police: a free, 24-hour hotline specifically staffed for English-speaking travellers — a good parallel or backup call, though not a replacement for 1669 in a medical emergency.
1367 is the Ramathibodi Poison Center’s 24/7 consultation hotline.
1199 is the Marine Department’s 24-hour hotline for water incidents (boats, ferries, accidents at sea).
This is Thailand-specific detail underneath the country’s own main emergency number, which this app already shows at the top of the SOS and hospital screens for whichever country you are in.
Comprehensive travel insurance covering medical treatment AND emergency evacuation (including from remote islands) is not optional here — do not assume your home healthcare system covers this.
Foreigners are charged for all medical treatment; there is no reciprocal free-healthcare arrangement.

Private hospitals — the fastest, highest-standard option — commonly want a deposit or a formal insurer "guarantee of payment" before non-emergency treatment. Even with insurance, you may be billed as self-pay until that guarantee arrives, which can take 24–72 hours or more.
Call your insurer’s assistance line as early as possible — ideally before admission, not after.
Malaria, dengue and Japanese encephalitis risk

Malaria in Thailand is concentrated in remote, forested border areas (with Cambodia, Myanmar and Malaysia) — the tourist islands themselves are low or negligible risk, and routine antimalarial tablets are generally not needed for an island or beach trip.

Dengue is different: it is endemic across Thailand, Vietnam, Cambodia and Laos, including all the islands, year-round with a rainy-season peak. There is no vaccine relied on for casual travel — bite avoidance (repellent, covering clothing, screens) is the real prevention.

Japanese encephalitis occurs countrywide outside Bangkok, peaking seasonally (roughly May–October), and is weighted toward rural, rice-farming areas. Vaccination is mainly advised for longer stays (a month or more) or higher-risk itineraries.
Anyone trekking into remote forest near an international border should get individual pre-trip travel-clinic advice regardless of the above.
