Not responding, or not breathing normally
Someone collapses, or will not wake up
Check for a response — speak loudly and gently shake their shoulders (a baby: tap the foot, do not shake).
If they respond and are breathing normally: do not move them if you suspect a neck or back injury; otherwise put them in the recovery position (below) and keep checking their breathing.
If they do NOT respond: shout for help, and check breathing for up to 10 seconds — look, listen, feel. Noisy, gasping or irregular breathing counts as "not breathing normally".

Not breathing, or not breathing normally: call the emergency number on speakerphone (or send someone to) and start CPR immediately — see the adult/child or baby steps below. Do not wait to find a pulse; lay rescuers are not asked to check for one.
Send someone to find an AED (defibrillator) if one might be nearby — large hotels, malls and airports sometimes have one.
CPR — adult and child over about 1 year
Lay them on their back on a firm, flat surface.
Heel of one hand on the centre of the chest (lower half of the breastbone); for a child, one or two hands depending on their size.
Push hard and fast: adult depth 5–6 cm, child about one-third of the chest’s depth (roughly 5 cm) — both at 100–120 pushes per minute, letting the chest fully rise between pushes.

If trained and willing: 30 pushes, then 2 rescue breaths, repeating (children may be given 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers). If untrained, unwilling, or unable to give breaths: continuous push-only CPR is still far better than nothing.
Use an AED the moment one arrives and follow its voice prompts — it will not shock unless a shock is needed.
Keep going until the person starts breathing normally, professional help takes over, or you are physically unable to continue.

Alone with no phone: with an adult, call first, then start CPR. With a child, current guidance is to give CPR for about one to two minutes first if you truly cannot call and compress at the same time (put the phone on speaker and start compressions the moment you have dialled, if that is possible instead).

A rescuer taught with breaths first (5 initial breaths before compressions, still taught in the UK/Europe for children) and one taught compressions-first (the US/AHA approach) are both following a currently-endorsed method — do not hesitate over which to use.
Lay the baby on their back on a firm surface, head in a neutral position (not tilted back).
For rescue breaths, your mouth covers the baby’s mouth AND nose.

Compress the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line, using two thumbs wrapped around the chest (preferred where you can manage it) or the heel of one hand if you cannot encircle the chest — two fingers is also still taught in some countries and is not wrong if that is what you learned.
Push at least one-third of the chest’s depth (about 4 cm), 100–120 per minute.
30 compressions to 2 breaths for a single rescuer; 15:2 if there are two trained rescuers.
Keep going until the baby responds, help takes over, or you cannot continue.

Which hand technique is "correct" is genuinely still shifting between countries as of 2026 — two-thumb encircling is now preferred almost everywhere, but two-finger and heel-of-one-hand are still taught and are not mistakes.
Choking — adult and child over about 1 year
If they can cough, speak or breathe: encourage coughing and do nothing else yet.
If they cannot cough, speak or breathe: give up to 5 firm blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand.

Not cleared: give up to 5 abdominal thrusts — stand behind them, fist just above the navel, pull sharply inward and upward. (Some countries — Australia and New Zealand — teach chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts; both are recognised as effective.)
Keep alternating 5 back blows with 5 thrusts until the object clears or the person becomes unresponsive.
If they become unresponsive: lower them to the ground and start CPR (above) — look in the mouth each time you open the airway and only remove an object you can actually see.
Anyone who was given abdominal thrusts should see a doctor afterwards, even once the object is out — they can cause internal injury.
Never do a blind finger sweep of the mouth.
Lay the baby face down along your forearm or thigh, head lower than their chest, supporting the head and jaw.
Give up to 5 firm back blows between the shoulder blades with the heel of your hand, checking between each.

Not cleared: turn the baby face up (still head-down along your arm/thigh) and give up to 5 chest thrusts on the lower half of the breastbone, just below the nipple line — two fingers, two thumbs, or the heel of one hand are all currently taught; use whichever you know.
Keep alternating 5 back blows with 5 chest thrusts.
If the baby becomes unresponsive: start baby CPR (above) and get emergency help.
Never give abdominal thrusts to a baby — real risk of internal injury.
Never do a blind finger sweep; only remove an object you can actually see.

For someone unresponsive but breathing normally, with no reason to suspect CPR or serious bleeding is needed: roll them onto their side and tilt the head back slightly, so the airway stays open and fluid can drain out. Do not put them on their back.
A baby: do not put them on the floor — hold them face down along your forearm, head supported and tilted a little lower than the body.
Keep watching their breathing until help arrives. Noisy, irregular or gasping breathing is a sign to treat them as not breathing and start CPR instead.
A pregnant woman should go on her LEFT side.
Do not swim out to them unless you are trained for water rescue — reach with a pole, branch or rope, or throw something that floats, instead.

Once they are out of the water and not breathing normally: open the airway and give a few rescue breaths (guidance ranges from 2 to 5; 5 is now the most common number taught), then continue CPR at the normal ratio (30 compressions to 2 breaths).

Untrained, unwilling or unable to give breaths: compression-only CPR is still far better than nothing, but breaths genuinely improve survival after drowning specifically, more than in an ordinary adult cardiac arrest — give them if you can.
Vomiting is common during resuscitation — be ready to roll the person onto their side and clear the mouth, then continue.

Everyone who was pulled from the water unresponsive, needed rescue breaths or CPR, or has any cough, breathlessness, confusion or drowsiness afterwards must be seen at a hospital, even if they seem to recover — a delayed reaction (secondary drowning) is real.

Sudden breathing or circulation trouble after a food, sting or medicine: swelling of the tongue or throat, noisy or difficult breathing, a wheeze or persistent cough, a hoarse voice, difficulty swallowing, dizziness or collapse.
Often — but not always — with hives or skin swelling. A reaction can be severe with no skin signs at all.
In babies and young children specifically: sudden pale, floppy or limp, not responding normally.
If an adrenaline (epinephrine) auto-injector is available, use it AT ONCE into the outer mid-thigh — through clothing is fine.
Call the emergency number straight away.
Lie the person flat and raise their legs; if breathing is very hard, let them sit up instead. Someone pregnant should lie on her left side.
Do not let them stand or walk, even once they feel better — a sudden drop in blood pressure while upright can be fatal.
No improvement after about 5 minutes and a second auto-injector is available: give the second dose.
Go to hospital every time, even after a full recovery — symptoms can return hours later (a biphasic reaction).

If in genuine doubt whether it is anaphylaxis, every source agrees: give the adrenaline. The risk of a dose given when it was not strictly needed is far smaller than the risk of withholding it when it was.
Lay a baby or toddler flat — never hold them upright.
Use their own prescribed auto-injector at its prescribed dose the moment anaphylaxis is suspected.
Auto-injector doses run roughly: 0.1 mg for about 7.5–15 kg (where that device exists), 0.15 mg from about 7.5–20 kg up to 30 kg depending on country and device, 0.3 mg above about 20–30 kg.
Under about 7.5 kg, or any child with no prescribed device: call the emergency number immediately and let paramedics or a doctor decide the dose — do not improvise with a mismatched adult device.
Dosing bands genuinely differ between countries and auto-injector brands — this is not a single fixed number worldwide. Always follow the child’s own prescribed device and plan where one exists.
Help them sit upright — never lie them down. Stay calm; anxiety worsens breathing.
Use the blue/grey reliever inhaler at once, with a spacer if one is available.
They have their own written asthma action plan: follow its dosing exactly.

No plan: either recognised approach is safe — 1 puff every 30–60 seconds up to 10 puffs (UK-style), or 4 puffs (one at a time via a spacer, 4 breaths each), wait 4 minutes, then repeat (Australia-style).

Call the emergency number if: there is no inhaler, the inhaler is not helping, lips or fingers turn blue, the person is exhausted or confused, breathing becomes quiet or slow, or symptoms have not resolved after the full first round.
Apply firm, continuous direct pressure over the wound with whatever is available — a cloth, clothing, your hand.

Life-threatening limb bleeding not controlled by pressure: apply a tourniquet a few centimetres above the wound — never over a joint — and tighten until the bleeding stops. Note the exact time it went on and do not loosen it.
A deep wound somewhere a tourniquet cannot go (neck, groin, armpit): pack the wound firmly and press.
Call the emergency number for any severe bleeding.

A proper manufactured tourniquet is best; sources genuinely disagree on improvising one from a belt or scarf as a last resort — most say it is better than nothing for life-threatening limb bleeding, one major source (Mayo Clinic) advises against it. If a limb is bleeding life-threateningly and nothing manufactured exists, an improvised tourniquet — a firm, wide band tightened with a rigid object — is the safer choice for most authorities.
Signs: pale, cold, clammy skin, rapid weak pulse, rapid shallow breathing, confusion or weakness.
Treat the visible cause (e.g. control any bleeding).
Lie the person down; raise their legs if there is no injury (a leg fracture or suspected spinal injury) that raising them would make worse.
Keep them warm, loosen tight clothing, give nothing to eat or drink.
Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible — still worth doing up to about 3 hours after the burn.
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with cling film (not wrapped tightly around a limb) or a clean, non-fluffy dressing.
Chemical burn: flush continuously with plenty of water.
See a doctor for: a burn larger than the person’s palm; on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a major joint; any blistering burn in a baby or young child; or any electrical or chemical burn.
No ice, butter, toothpaste, creams or oils.
Heat stroke — confusion, agitation, drowsiness, collapse, hot skin that has STOPPED sweating, seizures: this is a medical emergency. Call for help and start cooling immediately.
Whole-body cold-water immersion (up to the neck) is the fastest method if available. If not: pour or soak with cold water and fan the person, with ice packs at the neck, armpits and groin.
Do not give anything to drink if the person is confused or not fully alert.
Heat exhaustion (milder — heavy sweating, tiredness, headache, nausea, still alert): move to shade, cool the skin, sip water or an oral rehydration/sports drink.
Protect them from injury — move hazards away; do not move the person unless they are somewhere dangerous.
Cushion the head; do not restrain them; put nothing in the mouth.
Once the jerking stops, place them in the recovery position (above).
Call the emergency number if: it lasts longer than 5 minutes, it repeats, it is their first ever seizure, they are injured, in water, pregnant, diabetic, or not waking up afterwards.
Febrile seizures in young children: same basic first aid — never put the child in a cold bath or undress them to bring a fever down.

Do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger. Keep the head and neck as still as possible.
A motorcycle helmet: leave it on unless you need to remove it to clear the airway or because they are not breathing.

Get to hospital for: repeated vomiting, increasing drowsiness or confusion, a worsening or persistent severe headache, a seizure, clear or blood-stained fluid from the nose or ears, or unequal pupil size.
Call the emergency number — do not delay this to find aspirin or for any other reason.
Help the person sit down and rest in a comfortable position.

Lie the person down; raise their legs if there is no injury (a leg fracture or suspected spinal injury) that raising them would make worse.
Keep them warm, loosen tight clothing, give nothing to eat or drink.
Cool with cool (not ice-cold) running water for 20 minutes, starting as soon as possible — still worth doing up to about 3 hours after the burn.
Remove jewellery and clothing near the burn unless it is stuck to the skin.
Cover loosely with cling film (not wrapped tightly around a limb) or a clean, non-fluffy dressing.

See a doctor for: a burn larger than the person’s palm; on the face, hands, feet, genitals or a major joint; any blistering burn in a baby or young child; or any electrical or chemical burn.
No ice, butter, toothpaste, creams or oils.

Protect them from injury — move hazards away; do not move the person unless they are somewhere dangerous.
Cushion the head; do not restrain them; put nothing in the mouth.

Do not move the person unless they are in immediate danger. Keep the head and neck as still as possible.
A motorcycle helmet: leave it on unless you need to remove it to clear the airway or because they are not breathing.

Get to hospital for: repeated vomiting, increasing drowsiness or confusion, a worsening or persistent severe headache, a seizure, clear or blood-stained fluid from the nose or ears, or unequal pupil size.
Call the emergency number — do not delay this to find aspirin or for any other reason.
Help the person sit down and rest in a comfortable position.

If they are not allergic to aspirin, have no bleeding disorder, and have not already taken a full dose: have them chew an aspirin while waiting for help (chew a dose in the 150–500 mg range — 300 mg is standard in the UK, 162–325 mg in the US).

Give nothing by mouth — food, drink or medicine — until swallowing has been medically checked.

Red flags in a baby or child — get emergency care now
Does not respond normally, is very hard to wake, or is floppy.
Blue, grey, very pale or blotchy skin or lips.
Struggling to breathe — grunting, sucking in around the ribs, or pauses in breathing.
A rash that does not fade when a glass is pressed against it.
Signs of dehydration: sunken eyes, no tears, dry mouth, very few wet nappies, a sunken soft spot.
A bulging soft spot (fontanelle), a stiff neck, or a high-pitched, weak or continuous cry.
Give oral rehydration solution (ORS) in small, frequent sips. Keep breastfeeding or feeding as normal.
No ORS packet available: 6 level teaspoons of sugar and half a level teaspoon of salt, dissolved in 1 litre of clean water — measure the salt carefully, too much can be harmful.
Zinc supplementation, where advised: 10 mg/day under 6 months, 20 mg/day over 6 months, for 10–14 days.

Dose strictly by your child’s weight, following the pack or a doctor/pharmacist’s instructions.

Never give aspirin to anyone under 19 unless a doctor specifically prescribes it — the risk is Reye’s syndrome.

Watch especially as a fever comes down (usually 24–48 hours after it breaks, around days 3–7 of illness) for: severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting (3 or more times in 24 hours), bleeding gums or nose, blood in vomit or stool, extreme tiredness, restlessness or irritability, rapid breathing, cold or clammy skin.
Any one of these means urgent medical care now.
While waiting: paracetamol only, and keep the person drinking fluids.
Babies and young children are at extra risk of severe dengue.
Call the emergency number, or Thailand’s Ramathibodi Poison Center (1367, 24/7), and bring the container or packaging with you.
A swallowed button battery is an emergency: go straight to hospital, do not wait.

Over 1 year old, and the battery was swallowed within the last 12 hours, and the child can swallow normally: 10 mL (2 teaspoons) of honey by mouth every 10 minutes, up to 6 doses, on the way to hospital — this must never delay getting there.
Never give honey to a child under 1 year — botulism risk.
Constant, within-arm’s-reach supervision by one sober adult with no other task, whenever a child is in, on or near any water — pool, sea, river, even a bath.
A properly fitted, approved child life jacket on boats or in open water.
Drowning is fast and silent, not splashy — it can happen in seconds with no cry for help.
Sun and heat with a baby
Keep babies under 6 months out of direct sun — shade, an umbrella or the stroller canopy, and light clothing are the main protection.
If shade or clothing genuinely is not possible, a small amount of sunscreen on exposed skin such as the face is acceptable under 6 months.
Exclusively breastfed babies under 6 months do not need extra water, even in heat. Formula-fed babies may be given small amounts of cooled boiled water between feeds in hot weather.
Watch for: fewer wet nappies, dark urine, dry mouth, no tears, unusual sleepiness or fussiness, hot/flushed skin — get medical help if these appear.

Under 2 months: no repellent at all — use a mosquito net over the cot or stroller, screened rooms and covering clothing instead.
From 2 months: DEET up to 30% or picaridin are safe and effective (some countries, e.g. Canada, are more conservative and cap DEET at 10% for young children — check local guidance).
No oil of lemon eucalyptus (PMD) under 3 years.
Apply to your own hands first, then to the child’s face, avoiding eyes and mouth — or apply to clothing instead. Avoid the child’s hands.
Move away from the snake. Keep the person calm and lying as still as possible — movement and panic speed venom through the body.
Immobilise the bitten limb with a splint or sling. Remove rings, watches and tight clothing before swelling starts.
Get to a hospital that can give antivenom as fast as possible.

If trained in it: a firm pressure bandage over the whole limb (pressure-immobilisation), plus the splint, is the preferred field technique in this region when the snake cannot be identified — but only if you know how, and never at the cost of delaying transport.
Paracetamol, not aspirin or NSAIDs, if pain relief is needed — NSAIDs can worsen bleeding.
Do not cut the wound or try to suck out venom.
Do not apply a tight tourniquet, ice, an electric shock, alcohol or herbal remedies.
Do not try to catch or kill the snake — a photo from a safe distance is fine, but never delay travel to identify it.
Washing the wound is fine and even sensible; do not scrub it or apply anything else to it.
If not breathing normally: start CPR (above) — a box jellyfish sting can be life-threatening within minutes.
Pour plenty of vinegar on the sting for at least 30 seconds.
Then remove any remaining tentacles with tweezers, a card edge, or a gloved hand — protect yourself from being stung too.
Afterwards, for pain: either hot water or a cold pack may help — sources disagree on which is better, so use whichever is available.
Call the emergency number for severe pain, breathing difficulty, chest discomfort, confusion or collapse. Worse within 30 minutes → urgent care regardless.
Do not rinse with fresh water — it can trigger more stings.

Immerse the wound in water as hot as can be comfortably tolerated without scalding (around 45°C) for roughly 20–90 minutes, or until the pain is controlled.

Wash the wound thoroughly with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes (up to 20 minutes per Thailand-specific guidance) immediately.

Do not try to swim straight back to shore against it — you will exhaust yourself.
Stay calm, float or tread water, and raise an arm and call out to signal for help.
Swim parallel to the shore to escape the current, or let it carry you out until it weakens (usually just past the breaking waves) and then swim back at an angle.

Get out of the water and off the beach at once — do not shelter under a beach pavilion, umbrella or open-sided shelter.
Wait at least 30 minutes after the last thunderclap before going back outside.
A lightning-strike victim carries no electrical charge — it is safe to touch them immediately and start CPR if they are not breathing.
Calling for help in Thailand — beyond the main number

1669 (medical emergency/ambulance) is free from any phone, works nationwide 24 hours, and operators can usually handle basic English — say "English" as soon as the call connects. Response is markedly slower on islands and in rural areas than in Bangkok.
191 is police, 199 is fire — both free and 24 hours.
1155 is the Tourist Police: a free, 24-hour hotline specifically staffed for English-speaking travellers — a good parallel or backup call, though not a replacement for 1669 in a medical emergency.
1367 is the Ramathibodi Poison Center’s 24/7 consultation hotline.
1199 is the Marine Department’s 24-hour hotline for water incidents (boats, ferries, accidents at sea).
This is Thailand-specific detail underneath the country’s own main emergency number, which this app already shows at the top of the SOS and hospital screens for whichever country you are in.
Comprehensive travel insurance covering medical treatment AND emergency evacuation (including from remote islands) is not optional here — do not assume your home healthcare system covers this.
Foreigners are charged for all medical treatment; there is no reciprocal free-healthcare arrangement.

1669 (medical emergency/ambulance) is free from any phone, works nationwide 24 hours, and operators can usually handle basic English — say "English" as soon as the call connects. Response is markedly slower on islands and in rural areas than in Bangkok.
191 is police, 199 is fire — both free and 24 hours.
1155 is the Tourist Police: a free, 24-hour hotline specifically staffed for English-speaking travellers — a good parallel or backup call, though not a replacement for 1669 in a medical emergency.

This is Thailand-specific detail underneath the country’s own main emergency number, which this app already shows at the top of the SOS and hospital screens for whichever country you are in.

Foreigners are charged for all medical treatment; there is no reciprocal free-healthcare arrangement.

No signal needed. Hold the screen up to a driver, a hotel receptionist or anyone passing. The phrase is in the local script, so it does not depend on your pronunciation.
Not a ranking of quality. For a child, a pregnancy or a complex condition, telephone ahead so the right department is open when you arrive.

A monk’s vows forbid contact with women, including an accidental brush on a bus. He cannot decline politely mid-gesture, so the responsibility sits with you.
A raised camera is a question; a nod is the answer. Hill-tribe villages in particular have been photographed relentlessly, and a request costs you nothing.

Around a quarter of the population died between 1975 and 1979. Almost everyone you meet over fifty lived it and almost everyone under fifty grew up with it. The genocide museums and the memorials are where you go with that; a tuk-tuk is not.
As with the Thai wai, the height carries the meaning. A nod and a smile are perfectly acceptable from a visitor who is unsure.
Ask before photographing a person, a monk, a child, or the inside of anyone’s home or shrine.
At Angkor, remember it is an active place of worship: shoulders and knees covered, no climbing on carvings, no touching bas-reliefs, and no photographs of yourself posing in front of Buddha images.
Bargain in markets, never where a price is printed, and stop when you get to a price you are happy with.

Both fund the trade that keeps children out of school and, in the orphanage case, separated from living parents. UNICEF and the Cambodian government have both campaigned against orphanage tourism. Give to a registered organisation instead.
Carry small US dollar notes AND riel. Prices under a dollar come back in riel; a torn or heavily marked dollar bill will be refused.
Cover shoulders and knees at every religious site — men included. Carry a light scarf or a sarong.
Do not ask a Cambodian whether they lost family to the Khmer Rouge, and do not raise the period casually.
Do not beckon with your palm up and a curled finger, and do not point at people with one finger.
Do not climb on, sit on, or lean against a Buddha image, a stupa or a carving — and do not turn your back on a Buddha image to take a photograph of yourself.
Do not criticise the King, and be careful about politics in public.
Do not give money to children who are begging or selling, and do not visit or donate to an orphanage as a tourist.
Do not pay to photograph a chained, drugged or costumed animal, and do not photograph a slow loris held out for tourists.
Do not photograph or make light of the memorials at Tuol Sleng and Choeung Ek — no smiling selfies.
Do not raise your voice, argue in public, or let an argument escalate — even when you are in the right.
Do not show the soles of your feet to a person, and never point your feet at someone, at a Buddha image or at a photograph of a person.
Do not step over a person sitting or lying on the floor, or over food laid out on a mat.
Do not touch an adult’s head — or a child’s, however affectionate you mean it.
Every loris on a beach was taken from the forest with its teeth cut out and will not survive long. Paying for the photograph funds the next one.
Give and receive with your right hand, or with both — supporting your right forearm with your left hand is the respectful form.
Haggling is a normal, good-humoured exchange over a few coins, not a contest. Grinding a stallholder down over the equivalent of a dollar reads exactly as it sounds.
Holding hands is unremarkable in the cities; anything more is not, and rather less so outside them. Same-sex couples are generally safe in the big cities and should read the room in rural areas.
If you are a woman, do not touch a monk or hand anything directly to one. Put the item down within his reach, or pass it through a man.
It is the feet rule again, and it applies to buses, waiting rooms and restaurant benches.
Kissing and prolonged embracing in public.
Learn hello and thank you in the local language and use them constantly.
Losing your temper loses you the room and, in a dispute over a bill or a fare, loses you the argument. Calm and a smile are not politeness here so much as technique.
Palm-up beckoning is how you call an animal. Beckon with the palm DOWN and a scooping motion of the whole hand; indicate a person with an open hand.
Passing your lower body over someone or over food inverts the head-to-feet order. Walk around, or ask them to shift.

The kneeling-sideways position (feet tucked back, weight on one hip) is what everyone around you will be doing. Copying the room is always safe.
The left hand is traditionally the one used for washing. Handing money, a business card or a gift with the left alone reads as careless at best.
The monarchy is genuinely respected across the political spectrum, and there are lèse-majesté provisions. Political criticism carries risk for the local in the conversation, not for you.
The sampeah: palms together, a small bow. Fingertips at the chest for a peer, at the chin for someone older or senior, at the nose for a monk or the King.
The two currencies circulate together at roughly 4,000 riel to the dollar. Nobody will take a dollar with a tear in it, and ATMs dispense large notes that small vendors cannot break.
These are objects of worship, not scenery. Sitting on a temple wall for a photo is the single most common thing visitors are asked to stop doing.
They are the sites of mass murder and the staff have to ask visitors about this every day. Photography of the exhibits is allowed; posing with them is not the same thing.
Tip. Wages here are among the lowest in the region and a small tip is a materially different amount of money than it is at home.
Tipping is not expected but is genuinely welcome. Round the fare up, leave the coins, and tip a guide or a driver you were pleased with.
Topless sunbathing, and walking through a town in swimwear or with no shirt.
Two words, badly pronounced, change every interaction of your day. This app’s phrasebook has both, offline, in all four languages.
Wages are low and service charges rarely reach staff. Nobody will chase you for a tip; nobody will forget one either.
Wait to be seated and to be invited to start; the oldest person eats first.
What is rude, what is polite, and what is against the law — before you do it rather than after. Ordered by how much it costs you to get wrong.
When sitting in a temple, tuck your feet behind you and keep your head lower than any monk or image present.
A returned nop from a visitor is warmly received. Wait to see if a hand is offered before extending yours.
Accept “bo pen nyang” — never mind, no problem — and do not push. Hurrying people here does not work.
At the dawn alms-giving in Luang Prabang: if you are not taking part, stand well back, no flash, no blocking the procession, and do not buy sticky rice from the touts on the roadside to hand out.
Bargaining in Laos is gentler and quieter than in Thailand or Vietnam — a soft counter-offer, not a performance.
Do not criticise the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party or the government in public or online while in the country.
Do not touch a Lao person’s head, and do not sit higher than a monk or an elder.
Dress modestly and cover your shoulders and knees, in temples and generally. Lao women wear the sinh, an ankle-length wrap skirt.
If you are a woman, never touch a monk or pass anything into his hands — place it down or hand it to a man.
If you are given white cotton threads at a Baci ceremony, keep them on your wrist for at least three days and then untie rather than cut them.
It is the country’s governing phrase. A bus that leaves when it is full leaves when it is full, and visible impatience only makes you the problem in the room.
Laos is a single-party state with criminal provisions covering criticism of the state, and internet activity is monitored. As elsewhere, the risk falls hardest on the Lao person you are talking to.
Laos is the most conservative of the four on dress, and Luang Prabang has posted signs about it. A sinh bought locally is comfortable, cheap and quietly appreciated.
Prices are usually fixed in shops and negotiable in markets; agree a tuk-tuk fare before setting off.
Step OVER the raised threshold of a temple building, never on it.
Strictly observed in Laos. On a crowded songthaew, move rather than risk it.
The head rule is observed strictly here. If everyone else is on the floor, get on the floor.
The nop: palms together at chest height with a small bow. Lao people generally do not shake hands with each other.

The tak bat is a daily religious observance, not a performance. The rice sold to tourists is often old or unsafe and monks have fallen ill from it; some have stopped the procession entirely because of visitor behaviour. If you do want to participate, buy from a market at dawn, cover your shoulders, kneel, and do not make eye contact.
The threads carry the blessing that the ceremony called into you. Taking them off in the car afterwards is exactly as it would look.
The threshold is where the guardian spirit of the building rests.
A fork is not brought to the mouth in Thailand — it pushes food onto the spoon. Nobody will correct you, but the spoon is why the food is cut small.
Dishes are shared and put in the middle. Take a little at a time onto your own plate of rice.
Do not criticise, mock or insult the King or the royal family — in speech, in writing, or in a social-media post made while you are in the country.
Do not get a Buddha tattoo, and think twice about buying a Buddha image to take home.
Do not put an arm around a Thai person’s shoulders for a photo unless you know them well.
During Songkran, do not be annoyed at being soaked — but do not throw water at monks, at elderly people, or at anyone on a motorbike.
Eat with a spoon in your right hand and a fork in your left; chopsticks are for noodle soups. Sticky rice is eaten with your fingers.
Everyone around you will stop where they are. Carrying on walking is conspicuous.
Height signals respect, so wai-ing everyone at maximum height is not extra-polite, it is confusing. You do not wai staff who wai you as part of their job.
It is close to the head, and it is more familiar than it looks.
Jai yen versus jai rorn (a hot heart) is a real and widely-used distinction. Whoever loses their temper first has lost.
Keep a “cool heart” — jai yen. Whatever has gone wrong, deal with it quietly.
Loading your plate at the start reads as though you do not expect to share. The rice is the meal; the dishes are what goes on it.
Never step on a banknote or a coin to stop it blowing away, and do not deface currency.
Stand for the royal anthem — it plays in cinemas before the film and in some public spaces at 08:00 and 18:00.
Thai money carries the King’s image, so putting your foot on it combines the feet taboo with lèse-majesté. Pick it up with your hand.

Thailand’s lèse-majesté law (Criminal Code Article 112) carries three to fifteen years in prison PER COUNT, and it has been applied to foreigners. Third parties can and do file the complaint. This is not a matter of manners.
The Ministry of Culture has run campaigns against Buddha tattoos on foreigners specifically. Exporting an antique image legally requires a permit from the Fine Arts Department.
The wai: palms together, a slight bow. Return one from someone of your own age or older with your fingertips at your chin; return a child’s or a server’s with a smile and a nod.
Water on a rider causes crashes, and every year it does. The festival is genuinely for everyone otherwise, foreigners very much included.
Address people by title plus their GIVEN name — Mr. Nam, not Mr. Nguyen — and use both hands with a slight bow of the head when giving a card or a gift.
An unagreed ride is a negotiation you will lose at the destination. Fixed-price shops and supermarkets do not haggle.

Articles 117 and 331 of the Penal Code are used against speech, and the person who bears the consequences is usually the Vietnamese citizen in the conversation rather than the visitor. Let them raise politics if they want to; do not put them in that position.
At the Ho Chi Minh Mausoleum: no shorts, no vest tops, no photographs, no talking, hands out of pockets, and keep moving.
Bargain at markets and with cyclo and xe om drivers, and agree the price before you get in.
Do not criticise the Communist Party, the government or the state in public, online, or in a conversation a local could be held responsible for.
Do not open with the war. If your host raises it, follow; otherwise leave it.
Do not show anger at a driver, a vendor or an official.
Do not touch, lean on or photograph a family’s ancestor altar without being invited to.
It is called the American War here, more than half the population was born after it, and most people would rather talk about anything else with a visitor. The war museums are the place for it.
Look for the shoe rack or the pile. In the north it is close to universal.
Losing face publicly is a real cost here and shouting imposes it on both of you. A calm, smiling repetition of what you want works far better.
Nearly every home and many shops have one, often at eye level near the door with fruit and incense on it. It is not a decorative shelf; it is where the family’s dead are present.
Never stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
Seniority organises a Vietnamese table. Serving yourself first is the clearest way to look badly raised.
Take your shoes off entering a home, a temple, many small guesthouses and some shops.
That is how rice is offered to the dead — incense sticks in an urn. It stops a table cold. Rest them across the bowl or on the holder.
The guards enforce all of it and will pull you out of the line. Bags and cameras are checked in beforehand.
Vietnamese names run family name first, and about 40% of the country is a Nguyen. The given name is the last one written.
Wait for the eldest person to be served and to start, and offer them food first. Use both hands to pass a dish to someone older.
Cover up at dawn and dusk with loose long sleeves and trousers, and sleep with air-conditioning, window screens or a net.
Dengue fever is the most common serious mosquito-borne illness across all four countries. It is spread by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes and rises sharply in the rainy season.
Japanese encephalitis (rural rice-farming areas in the wet season) and Zika are also present; consider vaccination for long or rural stays, and pregnant travellers should seek specific advice.
Know what to avoid and what to do. Tap any animal for a photo, how to identify it, and first aid if you are bitten or stung. If in doubt, keep your distance and get to a hospital.
Malaria is a risk mainly in rural, forested and some border areas (not the big cities), spread by night-biting mosquitoes — ask a travel clinic about prophylaxis for those regions.
Most animals leave you alone if you leave them alone. Wear shoes at night, do not reach into holes or thick leaf litter, and never handle or corner wildlife.
Seasonal guidance only — there is no reliable real-time case feed here. Check your government travel-health advisory and a travel clinic before you go.

See a doctor for any high fever, severe headache or aching joints during or after your trip. Dengue needs rest, fluids and monitoring; avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, and get urgent care for warning signs such as bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting.
Tip out or cover any standing water where you are staying (buckets, plant saucers, old tyres) — that is where these mosquitoes breed.
Use a repellent with DEET (20-30%) or picaridin on exposed skin and reapply — the Aedes mosquitoes that carry dengue bite by DAY, peaking in early morning and late afternoon.
Guidance only — scams change and situations vary. When something feels off, walk away. If you are cheated or threatened, contact the tourist police.
The most common first-hour trick is an airport transport overcharge. The arrival guide lists the cheapest safe way into town for each gateway.

The only data that leaves your device is what you actively use online, such as a weather refresh, a translation, or tapping through to a booking site.

Save where I am staying on the map
Want data the moment you land? Buy a travel eSIM (e.g. Airalo, Holafly) before you fly and activate on arrival — a local SIM in town is usually cheaper for a longer stay.
Changing tables are rare outside malls and airports — a portable changing mat helps.

Cheapest at the big supercentres — Makro, Big C and Lotus’s (house brands plus MamyPoko / Huggies), far cheaper per nappy than 7-Eleven singles. Boots and Watsons pharmacies stock them too but cost more; Villa Market carries imported brands.
Heat and dehydration hit little ones fast: bottled water, shade and slow mornings.
In bigger cities, Grab and delivery apps can bring supermarket nappies to your hotel.
Pharmacies (Boots / Watsons in Thailand, local pharmacies elsewhere) are reliable for formula, wipes and baby medicine.

Documents are encrypted with your passcode and stored only on this device — never uploaded. Save your recovery code and an encrypted backup, and a forgotten passcode need never lock you out.
Moving from another device? Restore your encrypted backup, then unlock it with the same passcode.
You’ll get a one-time recovery code next — save it. The reminder below is just a hint, not your passcode.
e.g. my usual PIN + birth year
10-year, issued as 5+5, run by the Board of Investment
5-year, multiple-entry; 180 days per stay, extendable once by +180

Chiang Mai is the region’s biggest nomad hub, with many cafés and coworking spaces (for example Punspace and CAMP); Bangkok, Phuket and Koh Lanta also have coworking. Spending 180+ days in a tax year can make you a Thai tax resident — take advice.
Higher income and asset thresholds with more documentation; includes tax benefits on foreign income and simpler re-entry.
Proof of funds around 500,000 THB; you may work only for foreign clients, not Thai employers. Application fee about 10,000 THB.
Remote workers for foreign employers or clients, freelancers, and “soft-power” activities (Muay Thai, courses, medical stays)
Thailand has genuine long-stay routes for remote workers and retirees.
Use only the official government site — look-alike reseller sites overcharge and harvest data.
Visa rules depend on your nationality and change often. Treat this as orientation, then confirm on the official site for your passport before you travel.
Wealthy pensioners (50+, roughly USD 80k/yr income), work-from-Thailand professionals, high earners and investors

Cover up at dawn and dusk with loose long sleeves and trousers, and sleep with air-conditioning, window screens or a net.
Dengue fever is the most common serious mosquito-borne illness across all four countries. It is spread by day-biting Aedes mosquitoes and rises sharply in the rainy season.
Japanese encephalitis (rural rice-farming areas in the wet season) and Zika are also present; consider vaccination for long or rural stays, and pregnant travellers should seek specific advice.
Know what to avoid and what to do. Tap any animal for a photo, how to identify it, and first aid if you are bitten or stung. If in doubt, keep your distance and get to a hospital.
Malaria is a risk mainly in rural, forested and some border areas (not the big cities), spread by night-biting mosquitoes — ask a travel clinic about prophylaxis for those regions.
Most animals leave you alone if you leave them alone. Wear shoes at night, do not reach into holes or thick leaf litter, and never handle or corner wildlife.
Seasonal guidance only — there is no reliable real-time case feed here. Check your government travel-health advisory and a travel clinic before you go.

See a doctor for any high fever, severe headache or aching joints during or after your trip. Dengue needs rest, fluids and monitoring; avoid aspirin and ibuprofen, and get urgent care for warning signs such as bleeding, severe abdominal pain or persistent vomiting.
Tip out or cover any standing water where you are staying (buckets, plant saucers, old tyres) — that is where these mosquitoes breed.
Use a repellent with DEET (20-30%) or picaridin on exposed skin and reapply — the Aedes mosquitoes that carry dengue bite by DAY, peaking in early morning and late afternoon.
Guidance only — scams change and situations vary. When something feels off, walk away. If you are cheated or threatened, contact the tourist police.

A few features need a connection, and each one says so: refreshing the weather, currency rates, live translation, the “Across the web” rating and “Compare & book” links, streamed animal calls, and satellite map imagery. Weather and rates are cached after one online refresh, so you can still read them offline.

Almost everything works with no signal, because the guide is stored on your device: the phrasebook, places, food and produce guides, the wildlife field guide, fair prices, transport routes and schedules, border crossings, pools, your journal, trip, calendar, saved places, the document vault, and the base map (coastlines, rivers, borders and your pins).
Can I travel my way — with kids, a tent, or for a long stay?
Chabad of Thailand, Chabad of Cambodia and the Chabad center directory — only certified-kosher venues, never “kosher-style”.

Each place shows a guidebook score synthesised from public sources, plus an “Across the web” card with snapshots from sites such as TripAdvisor — each stamped with the month it was checked — and live links to compare and book. Your own rating always counts first: rate a place and it becomes the headline score and colours its pin on the map.
Everything here is guidance — always confirm prices, hours, service times and safety with the primary source or locally before you rely on them.

Everything you create — saved places, notes, reviews, pins, journal, trip and calendar — stays on this device only. There are no accounts and nothing is uploaded. The document vault (passports, tickets) is encrypted on-device; if you forget the passcode you can still get back in with the one-time recovery code shown at setup, or by restoring an encrypted backup. The only data that leaves your device is what you actively use online, such as a weather refresh, a translation, or tapping through to a booking site.

The only data that leaves your device is what you actively use online, such as a weather refresh, a translation, or tapping through to a booking site.

e.g. my usual PIN + birth year
10-year, issued as 5+5, run by the Board of Investment

Chiang Mai is the region’s biggest nomad hub, with many cafés and coworking spaces (for example Punspace and CAMP); Bangkok, Phuket and Koh Lanta also have coworking. Spending 180+ days in a tax year can make you a Thai tax resident — take advice.
Higher income and asset thresholds with more documentation; includes tax benefits on foreign income and simpler re-entry.
Proof of funds around 500,000 THB; you may work only for foreign clients, not Thai employers. Application fee about 10,000 THB.
Remote workers for foreign employers or clients, freelancers, and “soft-power” activities (Muay Thai, courses, medical stays)
Thailand has genuine long-stay routes for remote workers and retirees.
Use only the official government site — look-alike reseller sites overcharge and harvest data.
Visa rules depend on your nationality and change often. Treat this as orientation, then confirm on the official site for your passport before you travel.
Wealthy pensioners (50+, roughly USD 80k/yr income), work-from-Thailand professionals, high earners and investors

backTranslation.key: Open 24 hours
backTranslation.back: Open 24 hours

backTranslation.key: On the main Savannakhet–Hue/Dong Ha corridor with through buses.
backTranslation.back: On the main Savannakhet–Hue/Dong Ha route; direct buses run.

backTranslation.key: The beach is one thing and the street is another. Local women swim fully dressed. Even in resort towns, shops and restaurants expect you to put something on.
backTranslation.back: The beach is one thing and the street is another. Local women swim fully clothed. Even in resort towns, shops and restaurants expect you to wear clothes.

backTranslation.key: Losing your temper loses you the room and, in a dispute over a bill or a fare, loses you the argument. Calm and a smile are not politeness here so much as technique.
backTranslation.back: Losing your temper makes you lose the sympathy of everyone there, and in a dispute over a bill or a fare it makes you lose the argument. Here, calm and a smile are not merely politeness but a technique.
backTranslation.note: the idiom "loses you the room" read as losing everyone's sympathy

backTranslation.key: A fork is not brought to the mouth in Thailand — it pushes food onto the spoon. Nobody will correct you, but the spoon is why the food is cut small.
backTranslation.back: In Thailand the fork is not put into the mouth — the fork is used to push food onto the spoon. No one will correct you, but the spoon is the reason the food is cut into small pieces.

backTranslation.key: Busy with cross-border buses; the train crossing at Padang Besar is an alternative.
backTranslation.back: Bustling with cross-border buses; the alternative is to cross by train at Padang Besar.

backTranslation.key: What is rude, what is polite, and what is against the law — before you do it rather than after. Ordered by how much it costs you to get wrong.
backTranslation.back: What is rude, what is polite, and what is illegal — before you do it, not afterward. Ordered by how much it costs you if you get it wrong.

backTranslation.key: Cambodian e-visa or visa on arrival; a calm alternative to Poipet for Battambang.
backTranslation.back: A Cambodian e-visa or visa on arrival is a calmer option than Poipet for going to Battambang.

backTranslation.key: Roughly 07:00–22:00 daily
backTranslation.back: About 07:00–22:00 daily

backTranslation.key: What not to bring up
backTranslation.back: Things that should not be mentioned

backTranslation.key: Never stand your chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.
backTranslation.back: Never stick chopsticks upright in a bowl of rice.

backTranslation.key: Greetings and names
backTranslation.back: Greetings and names

backTranslation.key: Take off your shoes AND your hat before entering a pagoda or a home.
backTranslation.back: Take off both your shoes and your hat before entering a chedi (pagoda/stupa) or a house.

backTranslation.key: Laos is a single-party state with criminal provisions covering criticism of the state, and internet activity is monitored. As elsewhere, the risk falls hardest on the Lao person you are talking to.
backTranslation.back: Laos is a one-party state with criminal provisions covering criticism of the state, and internet activity is monitored. As elsewhere, the risk falls heaviest on the Lao people you talk with.

backTranslation.key: Links central Laos with Vinh; the bus route has a reputation for long waits, so travel by day.
backTranslation.back: Connects central Laos with Vinh. This bus route is known for long waits, so travel in the daytime.

backTranslation.key: Accept “bo pen nyang” — never mind, no problem — and do not push. Hurrying people here does not work.
backTranslation.back: Accept "bo pen nyang" — never mind, no problem — and do not pressure anyone; rushing people here does not work.

backTranslation.key: Quieter coastal crossing linking eastern Thailand with Cambodia’s southwest. The Thailand–Cambodia land border was closed to travellers after the 2025 conflict, and no reopening of this crossing could be confirmed in September 2026 — check before you travel.
backTranslation.back: A quieter coastal border crossing linking eastern Thailand with southwestern Cambodia. The Thai–Cambodian land border has been closed to travelers since the 2025 conflict, and the reopening of this crossing could not be confirmed as of September 2026 — please check before traveling.

backTranslation.key: bridge
backTranslation.back: Bridge

backTranslation.key: Nearly every home and many shops have one, often at eye level near the door with fruit and incense on it. It is not a decorative shelf; it is where the family’s dead are present.
backTranslation.back: Almost every house and many shops have this shelf, usually at eye level near the door with fruit and incense placed on it. It is not a decorative shelf but the place where the family's deceased dwell together with them.

backTranslation.key: Green-spored Parasol
backTranslation.back: Green-spored umbrella mushroom

backTranslation.key: Do not touch a Lao person’s head, and do not sit higher than a monk or an elder.
backTranslation.back: Do not touch a Lao person's head, and do not sit higher than monks or elders.

backTranslation.key: Roughly 07:00–19:00 daily
backTranslation.back: About 07:00–19:00 daily

backTranslation.key: Buy slow-boat tickets at the pier, not from bridge touts who overcharge.
backTranslation.back: Buy slow boat tickets at the pier, not from the pushy brokers on the bridge who overcharge.

backTranslation.key: The hat is the part visitors forget. Sunglasses too, if you are speaking to a monk.
backTranslation.back: A hat is what visitors often forget. Sunglasses too, if you are speaking to a monk.

backTranslation.key: Take your shoes off before entering a temple building, a home, and any shop with a step up and a pile of shoes at the door.
backTranslation.back: Take off your shoes before entering temple buildings, houses, and any shops that have a raised step and a pile of shoes at the door.

backTranslation.key: Articles 117 and 331 of the Penal Code are used against speech, and the person who bears the consequences is usually the Vietnamese citizen in the conversation rather than the visitor. Let them raise politics if they want to; do not put them in that position.
backTranslation.back: Sections 117 and 331 of the Criminal Code are used to prosecute the expression of opinions, and those who bear the consequences are often the Vietnamese citizens in the conversation, not the visitor. Let them be the one to start talking about politics if they wish. Do not put them in that position.

backTranslation.key: It is the country’s governing phrase. A bus that leaves when it is full leaves when it is full, and visible impatience only makes you the problem in the room.
backTranslation.back: This is the phrase that dominates the whole country. A bus that leaves when it is full leaves when it is full, and visibly showing impatience only makes you the problem in the room.

backTranslation.key: Do not touch, lean on or photograph a family’s ancestor altar without being invited to.
backTranslation.back: Do not touch, lean on, or photograph a family's ancestor shrine without being invited.

backTranslation.key: That is how rice is offered to the dead — incense sticks in an urn. It stops a table cold. Rest them across the bowl or on the holder.
backTranslation.back: That is the way of offering rice to the dead — incense stuck in a pot. It makes the dining table go dead silent. Lay them across the bowl or on a chopstick rest.

backTranslation.key: Kissing and prolonged embracing in public.
backTranslation.back: Kissing and long hugging in public

backTranslation.key: Do not criticise the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party or the government in public or online while in the country.
backTranslation.back: Do not criticize the Lao People's Revolutionary Party or the government in public or online while in the country.

backTranslation.key: Wages are low and service charges rarely reach staff. Nobody will chase you for a tip; nobody will forget one either.
backTranslation.back: Wages are low and service charges hardly reach the staff. No one runs after you begging for a tip, but no one forgets a tip either.

backTranslation.key: read this one
backTranslation.back: Read this item

backTranslation.key: The two currencies circulate together at roughly 4,000 riel to the dollar. Nobody will take a dollar with a tear in it, and ATMs dispense large notes that small vendors cannot break.
backTranslation.back: Both currencies circulate together at about 4,000 riel to the dollar. No one accepts torn dollar bills, and ATMs dispense large notes that small vendors cannot make change for.

backTranslation.key: Dress modestly and cover your shoulders and knees, in temples and generally. Lao women wear the sinh, an ankle-length wrap skirt.
backTranslation.back: Dress modestly and cover shoulders and knees, both in temples and in general. Lao women wear the sinh, a wrap-around skirt long to the ankle.

backTranslation.key: At the dawn alms-giving in Luang Prabang: if you are not taking part, stand well back, no flash, no blocking the procession, and do not buy sticky rice from the touts on the roadside to hand out.
backTranslation.back: At the dawn alms-giving ceremony in Luang Prabang: if you are not taking part, stand at a distance, no flash, do not block the procession, and do not buy sticky rice from pushy roadside brokers to put in the alms bowl.

backTranslation.key: Do not open with the war. If your host raises it, follow; otherwise leave it.
backTranslation.back: Do not open a conversation with the topic of the war. If the host brings it up, go along with them; otherwise do not touch it.

backTranslation.key: Far less hassle than Poipet and scenic, but transport is sparse, so plan onward travel.

backTranslation.key: The Apsara Authority turns visitors away for dress and has published rules after a run of nude-photo incidents. Skin oil damages sandstone reliefs that have survived eight centuries.
backTranslation.back: The Apsara authority has refused visitors entry because of how they were dressed and has published rules after several nude-photography incidents. Oil on the skin ruins the sandstone carvings that have survived eight centuries.

backTranslation.key: Box Jellyfish
backTranslation.back: box jellyfish

backTranslation.key: Thailand ↔ Malaysia
backTranslation.back: Thailand ↔ Malaysia

backTranslation.key: Do not open with the war. If your host raises it, follow; otherwise leave it.
backTranslation.back: Do not open a conversation with the topic of war. If the host brings it up, follow them; otherwise leave it alone.

backTranslation.key: Losing your temper loses you the room and, in a dispute over a bill or a fare, loses you the argument. Calm and a smile are not politeness here so much as technique.
backTranslation.back: Losing your temper makes you lose the sympathy of everyone there, and in an argument over a bill or a fare it also makes you the losing side. Calm and a smile here are not just politeness but a technique.

backTranslation.key: Look for the shoe rack or the pile. In the north it is close to universal.
backTranslation.back: Look for a shoe rack or a pile of shoes. In the north it is almost common everywhere.

backTranslation.key: Putting your bag or your feet on a seat someone else will sit on.
backTranslation.back: Placing a bag or feet on a seat that someone else will come to sit on.

backTranslation.key: Eurasian Wild Boar
backTranslation.back: wild boar
backTranslation.note: Eurasian Wild Boar read as "wild boar"

backTranslation.key: Officers at this remote post are known to ask for small unofficial “stamp” fees; expect it and keep small notes, or politely request a receipt.
backTranslation.back: Officials at this remote border post are known for asking for a small unofficial "ຄ່າຕີຕາ" (eye-striking fee? (?)); prepare yourself, carry small notes, or politely ask for a receipt.
backTranslation.note: "stamp fee" was written as "eye-striking fee" (a wrong word); fixed in this slice to the word for a stamping fee, in both places

backTranslation.key: Wait to be seated and to be invited to start; the oldest person eats first.
backTranslation.back: Wait for the seating to be arranged and wait to be invited to start eating; the most senior elder eats first.

backTranslation.key: Cone Snail
backTranslation.back: cone snail (?) (literally lime-pot shellfish)
backTranslation.note: Cone Snail read as a literal "lime-pot shellfish"

backTranslation.key: Do not beckon with your palm up and a curled finger, and do not point at people with one finger.
backTranslation.back: Do not beckon people with the palm facing up and the fingers curled, and do not point at people with a single finger.

backTranslation.key: The monarchy is genuinely respected across the political spectrum, and there are lèse-majesté provisions. Political criticism carries risk for the local in the conversation, not for you.
backTranslation.back: The institution of the monarchy is genuinely respected by all sides of politics, and there are provisions on defaming the monarch. Political criticism is a risk to the local people who are conversing, not to you.

backTranslation.key: Long-tailed Macaque
backTranslation.back: macaque (long-tailed macaque?)

backTranslation.key: Wages are low and service charges rarely reach staff. Nobody will chase you for a tip; nobody will forget one either.
backTranslation.back: Wages are low and service charges rarely reach the staff. No one runs after you asking for a tip; but no one forgets a tip either.

backTranslation.key: Do not criticise the Lao People’s Revolutionary Party or the government in public or online while in the country.
backTranslation.back: Do not criticize the Lao People's Revolutionary Party or the government in public or online while in the country.

backTranslation.key: Jai yen versus jai rorn (a hot heart) is a real and widely-used distinction. Whoever loses their temper first has lost.
backTranslation.back: jai yen (cool heart) as opposed to jai rorn (hot heart) is a real distinction and is widely used. Whoever loses their temper first loses.

backTranslation.key: The body is ranked head-to-toe: the head is the most sacred part and the feet the lowest and dirtiest. Feet aimed at a person say, very clearly, what you think of them. Sitting cross-legged with a sole facing someone counts — tuck your feet behind you or point them away.
backTranslation.back: The body has an order from head to feet: the head is the most sacred part and the feet are the lowest and dirtiest part. A foot pointed at a person says clearly what you think of them. Sitting cross-legged with the sole facing anyone also counts — fold your feet behind you or point them elsewhere.

backTranslation.key: Do not photograph or make light of the memorials at Tuol Sleng and Choeung Ek — no smiling selfies.
backTranslation.back: Do not photograph or joke about the memorials at Tuol Sleng and Choeung Ek — no smiling selfies.

backTranslation.key: Do not climb on, sit on, or lean against a Buddha image, a stupa or a carving — and do not turn your back on a Buddha image to take a photograph of yourself.
backTranslation.back: Do not climb on, sit on, or lean on Buddha images, stupas, or carvings, and do not turn your back to a Buddha image to take a photo of yourself.

backTranslation.key: Seniority organises a Vietnamese table. Serving yourself first is the clearest way to look badly raised.
backTranslation.back: Seniority order organizes the Vietnamese meal table. Serving yourself first is the clearest way to look like a person who has not been trained (brought up properly).
backTranslation.note: "badly raised" read as "has not been trained (brought up properly)"

backTranslation.key: It is called the American War here, more than half the population was born after it, and most people would rather talk about anything else with a visitor. The war museums are the place for it.
backTranslation.back: Here it is called the American War; over half the population was born after that war, and most people would rather talk about other things with visitors. War museums are the place for this subject.

backTranslation.key: Malaria Mosquito
backTranslation.back: Anopheles mosquito (malaria mosquito?)

backTranslation.key: Do not show the soles of your feet to a person, and never point your feet at someone, at a Buddha image or at a photograph of a person.
backTranslation.back: Do not show the soles of your feet to others, and do not point your feet at anyone, a Buddha image, or a photograph of a person, absolutely.

backTranslation.key: The nop: palms together at chest height with a small bow. Lao people generally do not shake hands with each other.
backTranslation.back: nop: press the palms together at chest level with a slight bow of the head. Lao people generally do not shake hands.

backTranslation.key: Loading your plate at the start reads as though you do not expect to share. The rice is the meal; the dishes are what goes on it.
backTranslation.back: Piling food onto a full plate right from the start looks as if you do not intend to share. Rice is the meal; side dishes are what is placed on top of it.

backTranslation.key: The two currencies circulate together at roughly 4,000 riel to the dollar. Nobody will take a dollar with a tear in it, and ATMs dispense large notes that small vendors cannot break.
backTranslation.back: The two currencies circulate together at a rate of about 4,000 riel to the dollar. No one accepts torn dollar bills, and ATMs dispense large notes that small vendors cannot make change for.
